item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-10-30
item.description:
• Cisco ASA and FTD SSL VPN reload flaw is exploited and on CISA KEV; fixes in every branch, no workaround. Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-28 fixes CVE-2026-76418, a logic error in the remote access SSL VPN of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD that lets an unauthenticated attacker reload the device with a crafted connection request when a tunnel group uses secondary authentication, and says Cisco's PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29. Cisco names no actor, offers no workaround and lists first fixed releases for every ASA and FTD branch. →
  • Lumen: Volt Typhoon's Silent Train relay chains fronted zero-days against SD-WAN, N-central and KACE. Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reports that Volt Typhoon ran exploitation, credential access and exfiltration through Silent Train, rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices that it rebuilt for each operation, and that its monitoring uncovered one likely and four confirmed zero-day campaigns against endpoint and network management platforms and SD-WAN orchestrators, among them Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, N-able N-central and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator. The reported victims are US-centred and the report names no Swiss or European victim. →
  • CrowdStrike: VAPOR PANDA runs ARTEX against 200+ organisations, European foreign ministries among them. CrowdStrike reports that from 2026-10-17 the China-nexus actor VAPOR PANDA used the ARTEX agent framework, driven mainly by the DeepSeek model, against more than 200 organisations worldwide, with the controller CrowdStrike saw directing exploitation in at least 14 countries, including foreign ministries in Europe, a European country's presidency, prime minister's office and defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities, and a Greek government entity. CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation at nine organisations, with the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor loaded by a renamed legitimate binary, and says this campaign is separate from the Storm-0940 ARTEX activity Microsoft reported. →
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01Cisco ASA and FTD SSL VPN reload flaw is exploited and on CISA KEV; fixes in every branch, no workaround. Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-28 fixes CVE-2026-76418, a logic error in the remote access SSL VPN of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD that lets an unauthenticated attacker reload the device with a crafted connection request when a tunnel group uses secondary authentication, and says Cisco's PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29. Cisco names no actor, offers no workaround and lists first fixed releases for every ASA and FTD branch. →
  2. 02Lumen: Volt Typhoon's Silent Train relay chains fronted zero-days against SD-WAN, N-central and KACE. Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reports that Volt Typhoon ran exploitation, credential access and exfiltration through Silent Train, rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices that it rebuilt for each operation, and that its monitoring uncovered one likely and four confirmed zero-day campaigns against endpoint and network management platforms and SD-WAN orchestrators, among them Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, N-able N-central and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator. The reported victims are US-centred and the report names no Swiss or European victim. →
  3. 03CrowdStrike: VAPOR PANDA runs ARTEX against 200+ organisations, European foreign ministries among them. CrowdStrike reports that from 2026-10-17 the China-nexus actor VAPOR PANDA used the ARTEX agent framework, driven mainly by the DeepSeek model, against more than 200 organisations worldwide, with the controller CrowdStrike saw directing exploitation in at least 14 countries, including foreign ministries in Europe, a European country's presidency, prime minister's office and defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities, and a Greek government entity. CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation at nine organisations, with the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor loaded by a renamed legitimate binary, and says this campaign is separate from the Storm-0940 ARTEX activity Microsoft reported. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 2Trending vulnerabilities 2Research, reports & policy 2Updates to prior coverage 5Action items 5

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures2 items

NOTABLENATOB3

VAPOR PANDA: CrowdStrike reports a China-nexus actor running the ARTEX agent framework against more than 200 organisations from 17 October, among them foreign ministries in Europe and a Greek government entity, and deploying the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor

CrowdStrike OverWatch reports that from 2026-10-17 a single ARTEX controller linked to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure directed exploitation against entities in at least 14 countries over 11 days, and that the campaign reached more than 200 organisations, including foreign ministries in Europe (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). One engagement focused on a single European country, its foreign ministry, presidency, prime minister's office and defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities, and another targeted 19 US organisations in pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, defence, nuclear and finance (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation at nine organisations and password spraying and credential scanning against at least 12 more, among them government entities in Europe (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). CrowdStrike states that the campaign is separate from the Storm-0940 ARTEX activity Microsoft reported and is VAPOR PANDA's first observed use of AI-driven tooling (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29).

The framework ran mainly on the DeepSeek model, with a human operator steering the agents at decision points while they pursued web, cloud, container, Active Directory, mail and VPN paths in parallel (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). In transcripts at a US pharmaceutical company the agent chained an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity flaw to query the cloud instance metadata service and obtain a role that could issue administration commands to thousands of instances; at a second it deployed web shells, abused an unauthenticated orchestration service for root in a container environment, read LAPS passwords and abused resource-based constrained delegation (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). Against a Greek government entity the operator supplied a 2022 directory export from the mail server whose authentication keys had likely not been rotated; the agent forged an administrator token, read mailboxes and used VPN configurations from a user's sent mail, with a VPN client key the operator described as coming from a May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). The operator also told the agents to find domain Windows hosts without the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). At a Middle East interior ministry and a Latin American foreign ministry the actor loaded the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor through a legitimate GameHook binary renamed svchost.exe that loads a malicious DLL (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). No Swiss target is named.

Exposure
Government, mail, identity and VPN estates where a directory export or backup holding authentication keys has never been rotated, SAML service providers that accept unsigned assertions, and cloud instances that still allow instance metadata service version 1; CrowdStrike names foreign ministries and government entities in Europe among the targets.
Detection
Telemetry classes are authentication logs (password spraying and credential scanning against many accounts, an administrator token minted outside the identity provider, VPN logins that use a configuration or key from an old mailbox or leak), cloud control-plane audit (administration commands issued to many instances through the cloud systems manager, instance metadata queries from an application), process lineage (a legitimate GameHook binary renamed svchost.exe loading a malicious DLL) and endpoint inventory queries for hosts without the security agent; CrowdStrike lists ARTEX-named command-line parameters, cloud roles and a directory under ProgramData as hunt markers (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29).
Defender takeaway
Rotate keys held in old directory exports and backups, require signed SAML assertions and IMDSv2, and hunt authentication and cloud audit logs for the parallel, many-target pattern an operator-steered agent produces; CrowdStrike expects China-nexus actors to keep adopting agent frameworks.

Sources: CrowdStrike

Silent Train: Lumen's Black Lotus Labs describes the rotating relay network Volt Typhoon used for one likely and four confirmed zero-day campaigns against management and control-plane platforms (Quest KACE, Versa Director, N-able N-central, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator)

Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reports that Volt Typhoon used a covert framework it calls Silent Train, first seen in late 2023, for the phases that need protection: exploitation, credential access, data exfiltration and continued access to victims (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). A session starts from a virtual private server outside the US, passes through compromised non-US SOHO and IoT devices and leaves through a compromised US device before the victim; more than 27 device classes were enrolled, from TP-Link routers and Netgear Orbi devices to Fortinet appliances and CyberPanel servers, and the enterprise platforms stayed in chains for one to three months as final hops (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). The operators exploit exposed web interfaces on the relay devices and deploy only what chained SSH needs, namely temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files and living-off-the-land utilities, with reverse tunnels over open-source proxies in later variants; sessions averaged about four hours, and at the end the operators removed all artifacts and dismantled the chain (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28).

Lumen says its monitoring helped identify one likely and four confirmed zero-day campaigns against endpoint and network management platforms and SD-WAN orchestrators: Quest KACE, where the activity looked like an undisclosed flaw, affected more than 30 victims and fell after Quest's October 2025 updates (a moderate-confidence assessment); Versa Director in 2024; the N-able N-central flaws CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876; Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN through CVE-2026-20127, exploited by late 2025 and after Cisco's February 2026 disclosure; and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator through the zero-day later designated CVE-2026-16812 (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). Post-incident analysis found in-memory webshells, credential harvesting and abuse of native platform features such as endpoint control and remote file transfers, and in several cases erased or altered logs (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). The victims it names are US government, telecommunications, defence-industrial, managed-service and critical-infrastructure organisations, concentrated in Hawaii, California and Texas, and it names no European or Swiss victim (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). The Hacker News carries the same findings from a report Lumen shared with it (The Hacker News, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
Internet-reachable management and control-plane platforms (endpoint management, SD-WAN controllers and orchestrators, out-of-band administration), and edge devices with exposed web interfaces, which can be enrolled as relay hops without any data of the owner being the target.
Detection
Telemetry classes are administrative logins, API calls, remote file transfers and configuration changes on management platforms outside normal administration hours or workflow, in-memory web shells that leave no file on disk, and, on edge devices, temporary SSH services, unfamiliar keys and outbound reverse tunnels to unfamiliar upstream hosts (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28).
Defender takeaway
Restrict the administrative interfaces of management and control-plane platforms to a VPN, jump host or management network and prioritise their patching, as Lumen advises, and treat an edge device that shows temporary SSH services or reverse tunnels as a possible relay in someone else's intrusion chain.

02Trending vulnerabilities2 items

HIGHCVE-2026-76418exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-76418, Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD: a crafted request to the remote access SSL VPN reloads the device when a tunnel group uses secondary authentication; Cisco reports active exploitation and CISA lists it (CVSS 3.1 8.6)

Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-28 describes CVE-2026-76418, a logic error in the remote access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD: an unauthenticated, remote attacker who sends a crafted request while connecting to the SSL VPN makes the device reload, and a successful VPN login is not required to reach the affected processing path (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026 and names no actor or victim (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29 (CISA, 2026-10-29), and CERT-FR restates the advisory (ANSSI / CERT-FR, 2026-10-29). The stated impact is a reload and denial of service, scored CVSS 3.1 8.6 with availability as the only impact; no code execution or data access is described (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

The first fixed releases are ASA 9.16.4.104 (for 9.16 and earlier), 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48, 9.24.1.27 and 9.24.10.1, and FTD 7.0.11 (for 7.0 and earlier), 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 and 10.1.1 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco lists no workaround; its mitigation is to remove secondary authentication from the tunnel group, which lowers the security posture of the remote access VPN, or, where DefaultWEBVPNGroup does not use secondary authentication, to disable the tunnel group list with no tunnel-group-list enable (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco confirms that Secure FMC, Cloud-delivered Firewall, cdFMC and Secure Access are not affected (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
An ASA or FTD unit below the first fixed release of its branch whose running configuration has webvpn enabled on an interface and secondary-authentication-server-group on any tunnel group; the default tunnel group DefaultWEBVPNGroup counts even when the tunnel group list is disabled. On FTD, read the deployed remote access VPN policy and the resulting configuration in FMC or FDM (Devices > VPN > Remote Access) (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
Detection
Neither Cisco nor CISA publishes an indicator. The mechanism points at device availability telemetry: unexpected reloads, HA failover flaps, uptime resets and crash files on units that terminate the remote access VPN, read against VPN authentication logs for connection attempts from external addresses that never complete a login.

Triage: a reload also follows upgrades, HA events and hardware faults; a reload that coincides with unauthenticated SSL VPN connection attempts from an external address is the pattern the stated mechanism produces.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade the units that terminate remote access SSL VPN with secondary authentication this week, perimeter units first; Cisco states denial of service as the only impact, so patching leaves no further step, and removing secondary authentication as a stop-gap trades an outage risk for a weaker VPN login.

vulnerability30 Oct 03:44Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Cisco PSIRT · CISA · ANSSI / CERT-FR
NOTABLENATOA2

WordPress core 4.7 to 7.1.3: an unauthenticated race in the core update process can lead to remote code execution, fixed in 7.1.4 and backported to every supported branch, with Wordfence reporting exploitation attempts and no CVE assigned in the sources

WordPress 7.1.4, released on 2026-10-28, fixes a weakness in the upgrade process that can lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window, and backports follow for every branch that receives security fixes, currently through 4.7 (WordPress.org, 2026-10-28); WordPress's release documentation counts 22 vulnerabilities, as Wordfence reports (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). During a core update with a complete package, the new files are unpacked into a predictable directory under wp-content/upgrade; the temporary copy includes the installer, and an unauthenticated attacker who requests it at the right moment can interact with the staged copy and reach PHP code execution (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). Wordfence scores it CVSS 8.1 for versions 4.7 through 7.1.3 and states that the attack complexity is high, because the attacker needs web access to the staging tree and must win a race that lasted only seconds in its lab (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). Patchstack reads the same flaw as needing wp-content/upgrade/ to be reachable over the web, notes that the sink dates back to WordPress 2.8 and that the window returns on every update, unattended ones included, and would not call it practical to exploit (Patchstack, 2026-10-28).

Wordfence reports that its new firewall rule matched within nine minutes of deployment and that it recorded more than 18,500 requests for staged setup-config.php installer paths in the first 21 hours, with two large sources polling small groups of sites for about 14.5 hours, which it reads as attempts to catch the update window (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). No source reports a successful compromise, and no source assigns a CVE identifier. The fix randomises the staging directory, adds an index guard and prevents unsafe promotion of staged configuration data (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). Most sites receive the release through automatic background updates, which Wordfence says should be checked rather than assumed (Wordfence, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
Any WordPress site on 4.7 to 7.1.3 that runs a full-package core update, automatic ones included, with wp-content/upgrade/ reachable from the internet; Dashboard > Updates shows the running version, and the fixed releases are 7.1.4 and the backport of each branch (7.0.8, 6.9.11, 6.8.12, 6.7.11, 6.6.11 and the earlier branches listed by Wordfence down to 4.7.39) (Wordfence, 2026-10-29).
Detection
In web server access logs, requests under wp-content/upgrade/ and for setup-config.php inside a staging directory, repeated from one source against a few sites as Wordfence saw (Wordfence, 2026-10-29); between updates the directory holds only an index.php (Patchstack, 2026-10-28). Where an update ran while the site was unpatched and the directory was reachable, confirm that wp-config.php and the database it names are unchanged, because the fix exists to stop unsafe promotion of staged configuration data.

Triage: a request to a staging path outside an update window finds only an index.php and is probing, not compromise; a successful response from the staged installer during an update is the event that matters.

Defender takeaway
Confirm that the automatic update completed on every site instead of assuming it, and deny web access to wp-content/upgrade/ at the web server, because a firewall that WordPress itself loads cannot block the request: the staged copy loads from its own files (Patchstack, 2026-10-28); Wordfence's blocking rule helps only where its firewall is set up to run before direct PHP requests reach their file (Wordfence, 2026-10-29).

Sources: WordPress.org · Wordfence · Patchstack

03Research, reports & policy2 items

ROUTINENATOA2

privatim revises its cloud guidance for Swiss public bodies (Merkblatt v3.02, 2 October 2026): sensitive data stays under the body's own keys, standard SaaS from Microsoft, Google, AWS and SAP is in most cases inadmissible for secrecy-bound data, and top management signs the residual risk

privatim, the conference of the Swiss data-protection authorities, dates version 3.02 of its guidance "Cloud-specific risks and measures" to 2 October 2026 (privatim, 2026-10-02); it replaces the version of 3 February 2022 (DCOD, 2026-10-27). For particularly sensitive personal data the public body must encrypt, the keys may be available only to it, and outsourcing such data, or data under a statutory duty of confidentiality, to SaaS from large international providers, with Microsoft, Google, AWS and SAP named, is in most cases inadmissible because of the untenable risk (privatim, 2026-10-02). Keys may stay with the provider only where no untenable risk follows and the provider is bound by contract to use them only with the body's express consent and to log every access (privatim, 2026-10-02).

The body, or its top management, is to confirm in writing that it has understood the risks and accepts the residual risk, and data the cloud services generate about their users, such as telemetry and logging data, is to be treated with the same care and contract terms as the content data (privatim, 2026-10-02). The five risk areas are contract design, places of processing including foreign authority access, confidentiality with encryption and key management, user data, and sub-processors (privatim, 2026-10-02).

Defender takeaway
The guidance addresses public bodies subject to Swiss data-protection law; a body that runs or plans standard SaaS from the named providers for sensitive or secrecy-bound data is advised to keep its own encryption keys, to have top management sign the residual risk, and to hold provider telemetry and logs about its users to the same contract terms.

Sources: privatim (Konferenz der schweizerischen Datenschutzbeauftragten) · DCOD
ROUTINENATOB2

ANNUAL REPORT: Cisco Talos Incident Response trends Q3 2026: public administration tied with finance as the most targeted sector, help-desk vishing into remote-management tools, and ransomware operators uninstalling and killing EDR

Cisco Talos Incident Response reports that in Q3 2026 financial organisations made up 18 percent of its engagements, tying with public administration as the most targeted sector (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Phishing was the leading initial-access technique at 37 percent of engagements and exploitation of public-facing applications second at 33 percent; the phishing cases include numerous actors who phone the victim as the IT help desk to get remote access allowed through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Ransomware and pre-ransomware cases were 27 percent of engagements, with The Gentlemen, Qilin, Rhysida and the closed group Interlock among the families and a new variant, VYPR, that Talos calls operationally immature: it had no leak site when seen, reused leaked Conti-derived source code and exfiltrated over several days (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29).

The VYPR intrusion began with a vishing call that had the user start a Microsoft Quick Assist session; the actor then used RMM software that ran PowerShell to download and install an MSI from a remote address, with MeshAgent, Rclone, PsExec, an IP scanner and mstsc as tools, and disabled EDR with several vulnerable drivers (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Interlock operators repeatedly tried to uninstall Cisco Secure Endpoint, used PsExec and taskkill to end security services and integrity checkers, turned off Windows Defender real-time protection and cleared event logs (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Talos names insufficient logging (over 40 percent of engagements), weak credential and secret handling, and absent or incomplete MFA as the most common weaknesses, and recommends centralised logging with at least 90 days of retention (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
An organisation whose help desk or staff can be reached by phone and whose endpoints permit Quick Assist or an unapproved RMM agent; Talos names public administration among the most targeted sectors in its caseload.
Detection
In process-creation and software-install telemetry, an RMM or Quick Assist session started after an inbound call, followed by PowerShell run under the RMM agent that downloads an installer from an external address; in endpoint and service-control telemetry, attempts to uninstall the EDR agent, PsExec or taskkill ending security services, Defender real-time protection switched off, vulnerable kernel drivers loaded, and event logs cleared.
Defender takeaway
Treat a remote-support session that nobody at the help desk started as the vishing signal and inventory which RMM tools and Quick Assist are permitted on endpoints; alert on EDR uninstall and security-service termination as a ransomware precursor; and centralise logs with the 90-day minimum retention Talos recommends, because actors delete logs on the endpoint.
annual-report30 Oct 03:46Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Cisco Talos

04Updates to prior coverage5 items

HIGHupdatedNATOA2

PK Softech, software supplier of Swiss pension funds: malware and a data outflow at Publica, with the City of Zurich fund PKZH saying its insured persons' test data was stolen, the Bernese funds BPK and BLVK and Pensionskasse Post also reporting the supplier incident, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office investigating

First published 2026-10-09 · open finding →

Correction30 Oct 2026 03:55 UTCrun 2026-10-30T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

The entry said that neither the Confederation nor Publica had named the actor. Publica's own newsletter of 2026-10-22 says the Akira group is being associated with the attack, and that Publica filed a criminal complaint with the Federal Prosecutor's Office on 2026-10-15; the summary, the sourcing note and the paragraph on the Akira reporting now say so, a population figure was trimmed from the analysis, and the demand and the Prosecutor's Office confirmation still rest on press reports.

Publica's own newsletter of 2026-10-22 says that the hacker group Akira is being associated with the attack, referring readers to the Federal Office for Cybersecurity's description of the group's methods, and that Publica filed a criminal complaint with the Federal Prosecutor's Office on 2026-10-15 (Publica, 2026-10-22). The same newsletter says Publica must assume that data left the supplier and that whether and to what extent Publica's personal data is among it is still being investigated (Publica, 2026-10-22). The ransom demand and the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmation of the exfiltration by Akira remain press reports.

Update30 Oct 2026 03:54 UTCrun 2026-10-30T0255Z-intelbodycvesevidencesourcessummary

Check Point's sk1000302 now notes a hotfix for the end-of-support R81.10 gateway release, published on 2026-10-29 at 11:30 GMT; the entry recorded hotfixes only for R81.20, R82, R82.10, R82.20 and Spark. The summary, the CVE records and the hotfix paragraph name it.

Check Point's sk1000302 carries a new note of 2026-10-29 at 11:30 GMT, "Released Hotfix for R81.10" (Check Point, 2026-10-29). R81.10 is an end-of-support gateway release that the sk still lists as affected, so a gateway on it now has a hotfix to install. The other hotfixes and the exploitation statement are unchanged.

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, HPE Networking ClearPass Policy Manager: bulletin HPESBNW05171 lists the 6.14, 6.12 and 6.11 trains as affected by the PHP2Shell flaws and names a hotfix patch for each (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

First published 2026-10-28 · open finding →

Update30 Oct 2026 03:53 UTCrun 2026-10-30T0255Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytitle

HPE's revision 3 of bulletin HPESBNW05171, dated 2026-10-29, exceptionally adds ClearPass 6.12.8 with a hotfix patch beside the 6.14.1 and 6.11.16 trains, and its affected-products note now reads 6.14.0 and earlier and 6.11.15 and earlier; the earlier wording that named 6.14.1 and 6.11.16 as versions with some mitigation is gone. The title, headline, summary, CVE records, evidence, action and text now follow revision 3.

HPE's revision 3 of bulletin HPESBNW05171, dated 2026-10-29, updates its affected and resolution sections to exceptionally include ClearPass 6.12.8 (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). A ClearPass 6.12.8 hotfix patch for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 is now named beside the 6.14.1 and 6.11.16 patches, downloadable from the HPE Networking Support Portal (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). The affected-products note of this revision reads 6.14.0 and earlier in the 6.14 train and 6.11.15 and earlier in the 6.11 train, while its machine-readable record gives 6.14.1, 6.11.16 and 6.12.8 as boundaries, and the wording of revision 2 that named 6.14.1 and 6.11.16 as versions providing some level of mitigation is no longer in the bulletin (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). The bulletin still says nothing about exploitation of ClearPass.

Update30 Oct 2026 03:52 UTCrun 2026-10-30T0255Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinereferencessourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitle

CISA added CVE-2026-97229 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29 and NCSC Switzerland updated its advisory the same day to active exploitation, citing Alpine Linux's report that a newly registered account crashed its GitLab 19.3.4 workers eight times on 2026-10-20 and 21, after which Alpine rebuilt the instance. Alpine also found that GitLab's fix is a patch to the Ruby bundled in its own packages and images, so an installation with its own Ruby needs Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9 as well, and GitLab's builds of 2026-10-21 also fix a second CVSS 10 flaw, CVE-2026-110264. The CVE record moves to exploited and KEV-listed, the summary, detection, takeaway and action are rewritten, and the superseded status lines are removed.

CISA added CVE-2026-97229 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29, "based on evidence of active exploitation" (CISA, 2026-10-29), and NCSC Switzerland edited its advisory the same day to add reports of exploitation attempts, moving the exploitation status to active exploitation (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-29). The report behind it is Alpine Linux's: on 2026-10-20 and 21 a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to its GitLab instance, which still ran 19.3.4, crashed the worker processes eight times and got partway through the exploit in four of them; the attacker returned on 2026-10-25 and 26 and failed, Alpine found no evidence that code ran but could not rule it out, and it rebuilt the instance (Alpine Linux, 2026-10-28). Alpine's upgrade to GitLab 19.3.6 on 2026-10-22 did not close the flaw, because the fix is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab applies only in its official packages and images, so an installation that runs its own Ruby needs Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9 or later as well (Alpine Linux, 2026-10-28). GitLab's release page now says its security team has released six threat detections for self-managed instances (GitLab, 2026-10-12). GitLab's release of 2026-10-21 (19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9) also fixes a second CVSS 10 regular-expression compiler flaw, CVE-2026-110264, so those builds are the better upgrade target (GitLab, 2026-10-21). Rapid7's statement of 2026-10-13 that it saw no confirmed exploitation predates all of this.

Sources: GitLab (Critical Patch Release 19.4.2, 19.3.5, 19.2.8) · CERT-EU · NCSC Switzerland (Security Hub advisory) · BleepingComputer · GitLab (Critical Patch Release 19.4.1, 19.3.3, 19.2.7) · Rapid7 · Rapid7 researcher repository (proof-of-concept README) · CISA · Alpine Linux (incident post) · NCSC Switzerland (Security Hub advisory, update of 2026-10-29) · GitLab (Critical Patch Release 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9)

05Action items5 items

  • Upgrade every Cisco ASA and FTD unit that has webvpn enabled and secondary authentication on any tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup included, to the first fixed release of its branch (ASA 9.16.4.104, 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48, 9.24.1.27 or 9.24.10.1; FTD 7.0.11, 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 or 10.1.1), internet-facing units first, because Cisco reports exploitation and its only mitigation removes secondary authentication.
    FindingCVE-2026-76418→
  • Take the management interface of every PA-Series and VM-Series firewall and Panorama off the internet now by restricting it to a jump box or trusted internal addresses, because Palo Alto reports active exploitation against internet-exposed management interfaces, and install the hotfix for your maintenance release, which Palo Alto's table lists for every line from 10.2.7 to 12.2.4 (11.2.10-h17 adds the Brotli fix).
    FindingCVE-2026-109618 +1→
  • Upgrade every self-managed GitLab CE and EE instance on 19.2, 19.3 or 19.4 to 19.2.8, 19.3.5 or 19.4.2 now, preferably to 19.2.9, 19.3.6, 19.4.3 or 19.5.1, which also fix CVE-2026-110264, internet-reachable instances and instances that allow open sign-up or public projects first, because CISA lists the flaw as exploited and NCSC Switzerland reports active exploitation; where GitLab runs on its own Ruby (a source install or a container image that does not use GitLab's packages) also install Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9, because the fix is a Ruby patch that only GitLab's official packages carry. On any instance that was reachable on an affected version, run the six detections GitLab published on its release page and treat the CI/CD variables, runner registration tokens and deploy keys of any hit, or of an instance where compromise cannot be ruled out, as exposed.
    FindingCVE-2026-97229→
  • Confirm in Dashboard > Updates that every WordPress site your organisation, its web agencies or its hosting suppliers run is on 7.1.4 or the fixed release of its branch, and deny web access to wp-content/upgrade/ in the web server configuration of each, because the race can be probed during any full-package core update and a firewall that WordPress itself loads does not run for that request.
    FindingWordPress 7.1.4 fixes an unauthenticated…→
  • Install the HPE ClearPass 6.14.1, 6.12.8 or 6.11.16 hotfix patch for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 on every ClearPass Policy Manager node from the HPE Networking Support Portal, and until it is installed take the guest portal and the CLI and web management interfaces off public networks, confining management to a dedicated layer 2 segment or behind firewall policy.
    FindingCVE-2026-109618 +1→
Verification & coverage notes1 run

2026-10-30T0255Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 6 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

A moderate window: six new entries and six changelog records. No deep dive and no critical entry: nothing met the stop-and-act bar, and the one candidate for a priority raise (GitLab CVE-2026-97229, now on CISA KEV) stays high: exploitation is reported by one observer (Alpine Linux, attempts against its own instance on 2026-10-20 to 26 with no confirmed code execution; CISA lists it and NCSC Switzerland restates the report), and the demonstrated path needs an account that can push to a public project. Reopen as critical on mass exploitation or a confirmed compromise.

  • KEV sweep (work/2026-10-30T0255Z-intel/kev-window.txt): CVE-2026-76418 (Cisco ASA/FTD) is a new entry; CVE-2026-97229 (GitLab, COVERED-STALE) is an update record that moves its CVE status to exploited. No RANSOMWARE row.
  • Backlog: the ARX Group SA row (Aurora leak-site claim) stays held. S4 re-checked it on 2026-10-30 (Ransomware.live press field empty, no victim, SBB, USTRA or Swiss press report in DE, FR, IT or EN); expiry 2026-11-07, struck then if unconfirmed.
  • Window: the previous intel run started 24 h earlier, so gap 24.0 h and window 26 h. The two earlier fires' attempts excluded 89 standard records from the slices; the breaches pool (20 records) was so small that S4 took its 12 oldest-cursor records without the exclusion, which is why bleepingcomputer, cnil-fr and similar records were swept again.
  • Mid-run stop-hook nudges to commit were noted and ignored: the run commits atomically in Phase 6.
  • Dates: Lumen's Silent Train page carries the metadata date 2026-03-16, but its text covers events through July 2026 and The Hacker News reported it on 2026-10-28; the new entry uses 2026-10-28 and an internal record corrected the same citation date on the KeyDrift entry.
  • Publica: its own newsletter of 2026-10-22 associates Akira with the attack, so a correction record replaced the entry's statement that Publica had not named the actor. The newsletter PDF extracts with broken line spacing, so the correction cites it inline and carries no evidence quote.
  • Single-source: Silent Train (Lumen's own research; The Hacker News relays it), Talos IR trends (first-party report), VAPOR PANDA (CrowdStrike telemetry and recovered controller transcripts), privatim guidance (the PDF; DCOD summarises), Cisco ASA/FTD (vendor advisory; CISA restates the listing). All carry the matching sourcing_note.
  • borderline-drop: Linux kernel CVE-2026-98432, patch-cycle class: NCSC Switzerland carried it on 2026-10-29 as a critical advisory with the exploitation status unknown, and Anthropic reports a lab remote-root exploit against MPTCP listeners with the code unpublished, but vendors rate attack complexity high (scores 5.9 to 8.1), no exploitation is reported, and no mitigation exists beyond the kernel update (Ubuntu and RHEL still unfixed on 2026-10-29). Reopen if exploitation or public exploit code is reported.
  • borderline-drop: Sophos UTM CVE-2026-118633, out-of-window: primary source 2026-10-28, window_hours=26; the 2026-10-29 BSI and ANSSI relays add no development, and there is no exploitation report; a pre-auth root flaw on an end-of-life appliance that needs a manual patch, so reopen if exploitation is reported.
  • borderline-drop: Progress WS_FTP CVE-2026-84295, unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 but no exploitation statement, and only CNA record text relayed by EUVD and GHSA (included with reduced confidence was considered and rejected: the vendor advisory is login-gated).
  • borderline-drop: Juniper JSA112183 Session Smart Router and Conductor, no exploitation, the 9.8 router row is limited to devices not yet onboarded, constituency deployment unknown, vendor page unreadable.
  • borderline-drop: Xerox and Fiery PHP2Shell (XRX26-016), out-of-window: primary source 2026-10-28, window_hours=26; no exploitation against printers, fixes from 2026-11-06.
  • borderline-drop: Oracle E-Business Suite CVE-2026-101767 (Canadian Centre wording of 2026-10-28), an authority restating open-source reporting with no first-hand observation; the entry already carries the Defused decoy attempts.
  • borderline-drop: OpenText Advanced Authentication CVE-2026-112256, a single CNA record via EUVD, vendor text unreadable, no exploitation statement.
  • borderline-drop: Microsoft's report of Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet using ARTEX (update on the Storm-0940 entry), two more ARTEX users in trend reporting; the Storm-0940 entry is already past 1,900 words, so an update record would add bulk for a marginal delta. VAPOR PANDA's entry references it.
  • borderline-drop: EFK audit of Microsoft 365 in the federal administration, recommendations on one tenant, no obligation or near-term action, primary 2026-10-21.
  • borderline-drop: Sophos GOLD OGRE and Aur0ra AI-agent intrusions; standard Active Directory chain run with AI agents, first reported by Gambit and CloudSEK in August; adds no new technique.
  • borderline-drop: Group-IB MadApe, SOCRadar n0n, Arctic Wolf Teams external-chat impersonation, Talos NIK C2, Cyble INJ3CTOR3 FreePBX, covered techniques or commodity capability with no victimology, vector or constituency exposure.
  • borderline-drop: OpenSourceMalware trojanized Claude Code extension, a single source that disclaims provenance; reopen on a vendor or second-source statement.
  • borderline-drop: EDK II PXE CVE-2026-97631, out-of-window: advisory 2026-10-22, firmware class, no exploitation.
  • borderline-drop: Binance theft (about 6.3 billion US dollars), global scale but nothing transferable beyond a preliminary "compromised engineer laptop"; reopen when the post-mortem names the vector.
  • borderline-drop: Polymarket and DebugBear script compromise, no Swiss or public-sector customer known; reopen if DebugBear names scope or a root cause.
  • Out-of-window items kept as developing stories (72 h window): the Silent Train report (2026-10-28), because it develops the KeyDrift story published on 2026-10-29.
  • Lookback: the privatim guidance (document 2026-10-02, announced 2026-10-13) entered through the dcod-ch lookback and is first coverage for the reader.
  • Coverage gaps: ox-security (article bodies 403 on every transport, lead-only); lab52 (feed SSL EOF, reader listing undated); resecurity (empty JavaScript shell on extract); golem-security (cookie wall, titles only); edoeb-ch-press (listing stale, sitemap recipe found); Juniper support portal, Progress and OpenText advisories (script shell or login wall).

Three candidates added (privatim-ch, ncsc-nl-php2shell-tracker, infostealers-hudson-rock) and three promoted to active (veeam-kb-security, dream-research, safedep).
  • For the next audit: the GitLab, PAN-OS and Publica entries are 600 to 1,160 words in the main text although earlier records grew them; this run shortened the GitLab and Publica text but did not rewrite them to the 550-word bound.
  • Verification: four iterations; iterations 1 to 3 returned NEEDS_FIXES (23, 10 and 4 findings, all remediated or declined with a reason) and iteration 4, a post-fix pass over 111 of 241 claims plus the full text of all twelve entries, returned one editorial finding (the WordPress firewall wording), which was remediated before publication under the low-residual early exit (truth plus editorial 1). No CLEAN iteration ran, so this publication rests on the early exit, not on a confirmed double-CLEAN; the next quality audit should give these twelve entries an independent pass.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-10-29
item.description:
• Talos: UAT-11473 implants KeyDrift in Cisco SD-WAN controllers through CVE-2026-20127 to collect data-plane keys. Cisco Talos reports that a cluster it calls UAT-11473 exploited CVE-2026-20127, the peering authentication bypass in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator (CVSS 10.0, fixed releases since February 2026, no workaround), and then ran the KeyDrift implant inside the controller's control-plane process to collect session metadata and what Talos assesses to be data-plane IPsec keys. Cisco's advisory, revised on 2026-10-28 to link Talos's post, says it is aware of limited exploitation, and Talos assesses with high confidence that the operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network. →
  • PHP2Shell: Trend Micro Apex Central and Apex One await patches to 11 Nov; Quest KACE and NetApp ONTAP have fixes. Trend Micro's advisory, last updated 2026-10-30, lists Apex Central and the on-premises Apex One server as impacted by the PHP flaws with critical patches due on 2026-11-11 and interim mitigations, shows critical patches for Deep Discovery Inspector and Email Inspector, and adds Mobile Security for Enterprise as impacted with a patch due on 2026-11-17; Quest says all KACE SMA and SDA versions are affected, with SMA 15.0 CU5 and 15.1 CU2 and the SDA 9.3 hotfix out and advice to block ports 80, 443 and 52230 until applied; and NetApp's advisory lists ONTAP 9 as affected only by CVE-2026-109618, with attacker access as the www user restricted to the PHP jail and hotfix builds from 9.14.1P18HF1 to 9.19.1P4. None of the three vendors reports an exploited case in what was read, although CISA lists both flaws as exploited. →
  • F5 BIG-IP is affected by PHP2Shell: fixes are in 17.1.3.7, 17.5.1.11 and 21.1.0.4; APM data plane and TMUI exposed. F5's release notes for BIG-IP 17.1.3.7, 17.5.1.11 and 21.1.0.4, each updated on 2026-10-24, list K000163821 as the fix for the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and call each a critical release whose only new changes are PHP fixes. NCSC-NL's record of K000163821 puts BIG-IP 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 and 21.1.0 in scope, through the Configuration utility of all modules and through the access-profile data plane of APM and SSL Orchestrator; F5's article itself could not be read, and nothing found reports an attack on BIG-IP, although CISA lists both flaws as exploited. →

  1. 01Talos: UAT-11473 implants KeyDrift in Cisco SD-WAN controllers through CVE-2026-20127 to collect data-plane keys. NCSC-NL's record of K000163821 puts BIG-IP 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 and 21.1.0 in scope, through the Configuration utility of all modules and through the access-profile data plane of APM and SSL Orchestrator; F5's article itself could not be read, and nothing found reports an attack on BIG-IP, although CISA lists both flaws as exploited. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 6Trending vulnerabilities 5Updates to prior coverage 9Action items 27

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures6 items

NOTABLECVE-2025-8088exploitedNATOB2

MDaemon mail server below 26.0.4 and Windows ClamAV 0.101.0 to 1.5.3: a crafted RAR emailed to any address runs code on the server through the bundled UnRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088, and ESET saw Russia-aligned attackers use it in Ukraine to deploy the HELLAGE and HELLTAG backdoors

ESET reports an active campaign in Ukraine in which Russia-aligned attackers exploited MDaemon mail servers and deployed two backdoor families, HELLAGE and HELLTAG (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). MDaemon uses ClamAV to scan attachments of incoming mail; old ClamAV versions carry CVE-2025-8088, the WinRAR path-traversal flaw ESET uncovered last year, which ESET says was fixed in ClamAV's source on 27 July 2025 (the release notes below date the fixed ClamAV builds 2026-08-07), while MDaemon kept shipping an old libclamunrar.dll until MDaemon 26.0.4 of 2026-08-25 (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). The chain ESET describes: a crafted RAR archive is mailed to any address at a vulnerable server, MDaemon invokes ClamAV to scan it, and the exploit writes a malicious DLL to the server's file system with no user interaction, so the message carries no lure (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). CERT-UA names the backdoors: HELLAGE steals email messages and other data, talks to a hardcoded server and can deploy more malware, and HELLTAG takes commands, transfers files and does reconnaissance through a hardcoded Telegram bot; ESET cannot attribute the campaign to a known Russia-aligned actor (ESET Research, 2026-10-28).

The exposure is wider than MDaemon. ClamAV's release notes of 2026-08-07 say it adopted the upstream UnRAR fix for CVE-2025-8088, which rejects path separators in NTFS alternate data stream names so that extraction cannot leave ClamAV's temporary scan directory on Windows, and that the issue affects ClamAV 0.101.0 through 1.5.3 with the fix in 1.4.6 and 1.5.4 (ClamAV, 2026-08-07). CISA has listed CVE-2025-8088 in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since 2025-08-12 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
An MDaemon server on Windows below 26.0.4 that accepts inbound mail (ESET Research, 2026-10-28), and any other Windows host that scans mail or files with ClamAV 0.101.0 to 1.5.3 (ClamAV, 2026-08-07).
Detection
Because the attack needs no lure, the mail log shows an ordinary message with a RAR attachment. The telemetry that matters is file creation of a DLL by the ClamAV or mail-service scanning process outside ClamAV's temporary scan directory, inbound RAR attachments whose member names carry alternate-data-stream syntax with path separators, and the mail service process starting unexpected children or connecting to Telegram's bot interface; these follow from the described chain and are not an ESET detection list. An update does not remove a DLL or backdoor that was already written, so check the server after patching.
Defender takeaway
Patch the mail scanning path first on any internet-facing Windows mail server, then look for unexpected DLLs and persistence and treat stored mail as exposed, since HELLAGE steals email (ESET Research, 2026-10-28).

threat29 Oct 04:46Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: ESET Research · ESET Research (APT Activity Report, April to September 2026) · ClamAV · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
NOTABLENATOA2

Moldova's government digital services: attackers used flaws in services reachable without authentication to query about one million national identification numbers and extract data on about 750,000 of them between 19 and 23 October, and the Prime Minister says AI allegedly helped find the flaws

Moldova's Electronic Governance Agency (AGE) reported on 2026-10-27 that between 19 and 23 October attackers queried about one million national identification numbers (IDNPs) through state digital services and that, on preliminary estimates, data sets for about 750,000 of them were extracted; MOLDPRES had put the access requests at about 11 million on 2026-10-24 (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27; MOLDPRES, 2026-10-24). AGE's technical explanation is that the attackers exploited vulnerabilities in services reachable without authentication and then used the data they obtained for further extractions; the first attacks hit an electronic service that logged the legal basis of processing incorrectly, which is why citizens saw entries for civil-status document requests and driving-licence issue in the data-access history of the EVO app (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27). Data that may be affected, not every category for every person, includes name, date and place of birth, first-degree relatives, insured status, family doctor, social benefits, pensions, disability, driving licence, photograph, vehicles and companies owned or run, IBAN, tax debts and payment history; AGE says card data is not held on the platform and it found no unauthorised change to state registers (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27).

AGE stopped the extraction on 23 October at 11:30, reviewed 82 digital services and suspended the exposed ones, and its timeline says 82 public services and more than 30 information systems and administration panels were disconnected as a precaution on 23 October; it blocked further attempts on 25 and 27 October, and the Prime Minister's account is that 30 of the 82 services were disconnected (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27; MOLDPRES, 2026-10-28). The Prime Minister says the incident is not isolated, that foreign state actors are being investigated and that the attackers automated the extraction, with the use of artificial intelligence allegedly facilitating the identification and exploitation of the vulnerabilities (MOLDPRES, 2026-10-28). Moldova has not attributed the attack to any country or group (The Record, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A public e-service of a federal, cantonal or communal administration that returns person data for an identifier without authentication, or whose output feeds other registers, since AGE says the extraction chained from unauthenticated services into further data (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27).
Detection
Citizens noticed the abuse because the data-access history in the EVO app showed processing for civil-status document requests and driving-licence issue that they had not made, so a data-subject-visible access log is a detection channel (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27). On the server side the relevant telemetry is per-service request volume and sequential or bulk identifier lookups from one source; the sources give no breakdown of the request pattern, so that is an inference from about 11 million requests against about one million numbers.
Defender takeaway
List the public services that answer for a person identifier without authentication and check what each one returns, whether it feeds other registers and whether its access log records the true purpose; rate limits and alerts on bulk lookups belong in front of every such service.

incident29 Oct 04:43Zsingle-source · victim disclosureOpen finding →
Sources: Moldova Electronic Governance Agency · MOLDPRES · The Record
ROUTINENATOA2

Machelen (Belgium) municipality: its own timeline shows a foothold through misleading instructions on an external website on 2026-08-20, found 22 days later after a high-privilege user was reached, with personal data confirmed stolen and Rhysida now listing municipal and social-welfare files

Machelen's own timeline records that on 2026-08-20 attackers gained access to an internal laptop through misleading instructions on an external website, explored it extensively from 24 August to 1 September, and on 10 September had access to a user with high access rights and other IT systems; the municipality found the incident on 11 September, isolated all systems, reported to the Belgian CCB-CERT, restarted part of its systems from a backup of a safe date on 14 September and recorded the first evidence of leaked data on 17 September (Municipality of Machelen, 2026-09-22). It confirms that personal data was leaked and says the scope is still being investigated (Municipality of Machelen, 2026-09-22); the mayor had said on 14 September that no personal data appeared to be affected, and ITdaily reports that this proved wrong (ITdaily, 2026-09-23). Ransomware.live recorded on 2026-10-27 that Rhysida listed Machelen on its leak site, describing the listing as municipal and social-welfare file servers of about 1.3 million files, with client files that include passports and identity cards, nursing-home medical files and civil-status records, which are the group's own claims (Ransomware.live, 2026-10-27).

Detection
The timeline puts 22 days between first access and detection, with the first laptop explored from 24 August to 1 September; it names neither the website nor the commands, so the telemetry to review includes endpoint process creation after a user followed instructions on a web page and later use of a high-privilege account from that workstation, which is an inference from the timeline.
Defender takeaway
Treat a user who followed instructions from a website on a work laptop as a possible intrusion that can sit unseen for weeks; review high-privilege account activity from the user's workstation for the weeks after the event, not only the day it is reported.

KeyDrift: Talos reports UAT-11473 exploiting CVE-2026-20127 in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN controllers to run an implant inside the control-plane daemon that collects data-plane keys, with infrastructure overlapping Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network

Cisco Talos reports that UAT-11473 exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass in the peering authentication of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28), and then installed a custom framework it calls KeyDrift (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). CISA has listed the flaw in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since 2026-02-25 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28). Cisco's advisory (CVSS 10.0) says an unauthenticated remote attacker can log in as an internal high-privileged non-root user and reach NETCONF to change the SD-WAN fabric configuration, and that there is no workaround (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco's advisory, revised on 2026-10-28 to link Talos's post, says its PSIRT is aware of limited exploitation (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reported on 2026-10-28 that Volt Typhoon had exploited the flaw since late 2025 and after Cisco's February disclosure (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28), and Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11473's operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28).

KeyDrift runs inside the control-plane daemon. The actor edits the runit launchers of sshd and of a look-alike aaamgr service and remounts /rootfs.rw executable: the sshd launcher starts a script that injects the PolyFlame library into every running vdaemon process by ptrace, and the aaamgr launcher runs a packed PolyFlame loader directly (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). PolyFlame is tasked in-band over the control-plane traffic and offers a command, file-write and file-read backdoor and an intermediate command relay; Talos recovered no hardcoded address, port or domain (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). A second component, LittleFilch, hooks SSL_read in vdaemon and collects peer system addresses and 32-byte values Talos assesses to be OMP-distributed IPsec data-plane keys, writing them RSA-encrypted to /var/tmp (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). Talos lists observed targeting as space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research, calls the activity historical and does not say how many controllers were affected (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
Every Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator regardless of configuration, on-premises or in Cisco's hosted clouds, on a release below the first fixed one in the advisory's table; Cisco says controllers with ports exposed to the internet are at risk (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
Detection
On the controller's authentication log, Cisco says to audit /var/log/auth.log for accepted public-key logins of the vmanage-admin account from addresses that are not among the configured System IPs, and to validate control-connection peering events, those of peer type vmanage first, against maintenance windows and asset inventory (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). On the host, Talos names modified runit run scripts that remount the overlay root executable and start a background script, an aaamgr service that runs a compiled, packed ELF, extra libraries mapped into vdaemon with ptrace activity against it and encrypted staging files under /var/tmp (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). Cisco asks for admin-tech files and a TAC case when compromise is suspected (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

Triage: an aaamgr service that runs as a compiled ELF is the discriminator, because the legitimate component is a Python package and does not normally appear that way (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to the fixed releases and restrict the control components' management ports, then treat any controller that was internet-reachable on a vulnerable release as a compromise-assessment target, because Lumen dates exploitation of the flaw to late 2025, before Cisco's February disclosure, and the implant runs in the process that handles the fabric's control sessions.

testmetest: an npm worm in the Miasma and Shai-Hulud family now starts when an application imports the package, so install with --ignore-scripts no longer protects, and JFrog finds 42 third-party GitHub repositories already armed with its publisher

SafeDep counts 19 npm packages from the same operator between 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-27, eight of them published through four npm accounts, that carry a worm sharing code with the June Miasma worm and adding the token-revocation wiper of Mini Shai-Hulud; SafeDep has not confirmed the lineage, and JFrog says its evidence does not establish that the original Miasma operators are responsible (SafeDep, 2026-10-27; JFrog Security Research, 2026-10-26). The install trigger has changed twice: first a command expansion in a binding.gyp file, with no install script; then a postinstall script that loads a native addon which decodes and starts the worm; and, since SafeDep's update of 27 October, an addon that runs when an application imports the package, so a hardening step that disables install scripts does not stop it (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).

The payload exits on CIS locales and in known analysis sandboxes. It steals SSH keys, registry and Git credentials, .env files, browser logins, AI-tool, cloud, Vault and Kubernetes secrets and GitHub Actions secrets read from runner memory (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). It exfiltrates by committing encrypted data, with the victim's encrypted GitHub token, to a new public repository in the victim's own account, injects a GitLab CI job that requests npm and PyPI OIDC tokens, adds its loader to the victim's npm packages and publishes new patch versions, republishes to PyPI and RubyGems, commits a fake CodeQL workflow and AI-agent configuration files that infect the host again, and copies itself over SSH to the hosts in known_hosts (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). A persistence service checks the stolen GitHub token every 45 seconds for 48 hours and on an authentication failure deletes the home directory (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). JFrog found 42 armed third-party GitHub repositories of 11 legitimate owners with hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, and says the payload blobs were large enough to evade GitHub's search and API paths (JFrog Security Research, 2026-10-26).

Exposure
Any developer endpoint, build agent or CI runner that installed or imported one of the operator's packages, and any GitHub or GitLab account whose token such a host held (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).
Detection
In package metadata, a binding.gyp whose sources field runs node in a package with no C or C++ sources, a postinstall that requires a .node file and discards errors beside a large high-entropy file, and prebuilt addons with no native source; on endpoints and CI runners, a node process that downloads or finds and runs the Bun runtime and a child node process started from a temporary path named after its process ID; in GitHub and GitLab audit logs, a new public repository in a developer's own account with a generic project description, commits with a fixed automated-sync message, commits that add AI-assistant configuration files (.claude, .cursor, .gemini, .vscode tasks, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md), an injected CI job that requests OIDC tokens, and unexpected patch releases of your own packages (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).
Defender takeaway
An install that ran with scripts disabled is not clean once the package has been imported; for an affected host SafeDep's order is to disconnect it, remove persistence first, rotate all credentials, check the accounts for the repositories and commits above and reinstall the operating system (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). Because the wiper is triggered by the token's revocation, the host is isolated and cleaned before the GitHub token is revoked.

Huntress: phished MDM enrolments in Hexnode and Rippling give attackers a management path that brings ScreenConnect back after it has been removed

Huntress reports several recent incidents in which attackers used legitimate mobile-device-management platforms, not flaws in them, as a trusted management path, naming Hexnode and Rippling as the two it saw and noting the list is not definitive (Huntress, 2026-10-28). In the first case, proposal-themed emails led a user to download an MSI named like a DocuSign installer that installed Hexnode components (gateway, agent and PostgreSQL components); ScreenConnect followed shortly after and connected to an attacker relay, the managed-service provider removed it, and it came back several hours later to the same relay while the Hexnode client was still installed (Huntress, 2026-10-28). In the second, a receptionist clicked a link in an email about tax planning that led to a fake Teams calendar page; about a minute later a Rippling enrolment registry key appeared, the agent was downloaded into a SYSTEM profile path and installed with SYSTEM rights, and about 35 minutes after that the attacker used the MDM to stage and run a ScreenConnect installer as SYSTEM (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A managed Windows endpoint whose user can run an installer or follow an enrolment link, in an organisation without an inventory of its authorised MDM tenants, agents and RMM instances (Huntress, 2026-10-28).
Detection
The chain Huntress describes as a stronger signal is social engineering, then a new MDM enrolment, then an RMM installation, then outbound communication with an unfamiliar relay, correlated across identity, MDM, endpoint and network telemetry; in endpoint telemetry that is an MSI run from a browser download folder that installs an MDM agent, an enrolment registry key on a device nobody enrolled, a new SYSTEM-level agent in a vendor directory shortly after a click, and an RMM installed by that agent (Huntress, 2026-10-28). A repeat of the same RMM relay after the RMM was removed, as in the Hexnode case, points to a remaining MDM client as a possible source (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Triage: a corporate enrolment started by IT looks similar in process telemetry; the discriminators are a tenant that is not in the authorised inventory, a trigger that is an emailed link or a user-run installer instead of IT's enrolment workflow, and an RMM install within minutes (an inference from Huntress's two cases).

Defender takeaway
Treat an unexpected MDM enrolment as a security event and keep an inventory of authorised tenants; after removing a rogue RMM, unenrol the device from the unauthorised tenant, disable accounts the attacker created, revoke sessions and tokens, reset credentials and reimage the endpoint if its integrity cannot be confirmed, as Huntress advises (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A Trend Micro Apex Central, Apex One or Mobile Security for Enterprise server whose console or web endpoints a hostile network can reach; any KACE SMA or SDA, whose web ports and agent port 52230 are named; any ONTAP 9 cluster whose web services are reachable and that runs a release other than the fixed builds (Trend Micro, 2026-10-28; Quest Software, 2026-10-28; NetApp Knowledge Base, 2026-10-26).

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Check Point Force, Spark and Cloud firewalls: the PHP2Shell flaws reach the web interfaces of gateways that run Mobile Access, SSL Network Extender, SAML-realm VPN, the Identity Awareness captive portal, UserCheck or Zero Phishing; hotfixes since 2026-10-23, the R81.20 package reissued on 2026-10-28 (CVSS 9.2)

Check Point's advisory sk1000302, created on 2026-10-21 and last modified on 2026-10-29, says that under certain circumstances the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both scored CVSS 9.2, may allow remote code execution through firewall web interfaces (Check Point, 2026-10-29). Affected are Force, Spark and Cloud firewalls that use one or more of Mobile Access Portal (not Spark), Remote Access VPN with SSL Network Extender (not Spark), Remote Access VPN with SAML realm authentication, the Identity Awareness captive portal, the UserCheck portal and Zero Phishing, on R81.20, R82, R82.10 and R82.20 and on Spark R81.10.x and R82.00.x; R80 to R81.10 and the older Spark lines are end of support and also listed (Check Point, 2026-10-29). Check Point's portal and SaaS services are already patched, Security Management and Log Servers are not affected, and its products are not vulnerable to the third PHP issue, CVE-2026-115560 (Check Point, 2026-10-29).

The hotfix, first published on 2026-10-23, implements the PHP 7.4 fix, is compatible with every Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator take, goes on each gateway, cluster member, security-group member or standalone server and needs a reboot; the R82, R82.10 and R82.20 packages were reissued on 2026-10-26 to support standalone deployments, and the R81.20 package was reissued on 2026-10-28 to fix a Mobile Access problem, must sit on take 166 or higher and is required where the Mobile Access Portal is used (Check Point, 2026-10-29). For the gateway packages the fix is also planned for the Jumbo Hotfix Accumulators of 2026-11-11, and Spark has R82.00.11 (build 998002823) and R81.10.17 (build 996004992) (Check Point, 2026-10-29); a hotfix for the end-of-support R81.10 gateway release was published on 2026-10-29 at 11:30 GMT (Check Point, 2026-10-29). Until a hotfix is installed, Check Point's mitigation is a block in cp-httpd.conf that denies requests with a multipart Content-Type, followed by a restart of the portals, which is removed before installing the hotfix; R82.20 gateways are also protected by the "PHP Remote Code Execution" IPS signature even when IPS is not enabled (Check Point, 2026-10-29). CISA lists both PHP flaws as exploited since 2026-10-26, and the sk makes no statement on exploitation of Check Point gateways (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A gateway on a listed release with at least one of the six portal or VPN features in use; a gateway with none of them is outside the scope Check Point states (Check Point, 2026-10-29).
Detection
Check Point publishes no indicator and no post-compromise check. The web daemon's access logs for the portal paths, shells or downloads started by the gateway's web process, and outbound connections that the gateway itself initiates are the telemetry to review on a gateway that faced the internet before the fix; this is an inference, since the sk does not describe the attack.
Defender takeaway
Install the hotfix on every gateway that publishes a portal or VPN; where it has to wait, apply the cp-httpd.conf mitigation, and treat a gateway that was exposed and unpatched as needing a compromise check, because Check Point's page does not say whether patching removes a foothold.

WatchGuard's advisory listing of 2026-10-27 opens with 18 rows, 17 for Fireware OS and one for Mobile VPN with SSL Client for Windows, and seven of the 17 are scored 9.0 or higher (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). The fixes are in Fireware OS 2026.4, 12.12.4 and, for T15 and T35 models, 12.5.22. Three of the seven need no authentication but a specific feature. CVE-2026-93866 (9.2) is an integer overflow in the WebSocket handling of the Access Portal that lets a remote unauthenticated attacker write beyond the bounds of a heap buffer while the Access Portal is enabled (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-93857 (9.2) is a stack buffer overflow in the SIP proxy that gives remote code execution when a SIP proxy is configured on the Firebox (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-93865 (9.2) is missing authentication in the FireCluster synchronization daemon: a remote unauthenticated attacker invokes privileged administrative actions with a crafted request to the FireCluster management IP when clustering is enabled (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27).

The other four need a network position. CVE-2026-112709 and CVE-2026-112710 (9.2 each) are heap overflows in the authentication service that give denial of service and possibly code execution to an attacker who controls or intercepts traffic to the configured Active Directory server and returns a crafted response (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-103594 (9.5) is a stack overflow in WireGuard configuration processing for a man-in-the-middle with TLS-decrypted access between a Firebox that acts as a FireCloud Gateway and WatchGuard Cloud (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-103593 (9.1) is a stack overflow in the logging service that gives root code execution to a network-adjacent attacker who impersonates or intercepts traffic to the log server with a crafted certificate, in FIPS mode (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). Six rows affect Fireware OS 2025.1 up to before 2026.4 and 12.0 up to before 12.12.4, T15 and T35 up to before 12.5.22, the WireGuard row starts at 2026.2 and 12.12, and each page states that WatchGuard is not aware of exploitation in the wild (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
A Firebox on a Fireware OS release inside those ranges with at least one of the listed features: the Access Portal, a SIP proxy policy, FireCluster membership, an Active Directory authentication server, the FireCloud Gateway role, or FIPS mode with an external log server; the three unauthenticated rows are reachable by any host that can reach the Access Portal, the SIP proxy policy or the cluster management address (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27).
Detection
WatchGuard publishes no indicator and no workaround. For the three unauthenticated rows, connections to the cluster management address from hosts that are not cluster peers, WebSocket upgrade requests to the Access Portal from unexpected sources, SIP traffic from outside expected carriers, and restarts of the portal, SIP or sync services on the Firebox are the telemetry to review; this is an inference from the stated mechanisms.
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed release on appliances with the Access Portal, a SIP proxy or clustering first; where an upgrade has to wait, turn off a feature that is not used and keep the cluster management address off untrusted segments.

CVE-2026-108142, Veeam Backup & Replication: an unauthenticated authorization bypass on the CDP Coordinator Service of 13.x backup servers (CVSS 4.0 9.1), fixed in 13.1.2 and 13.0.3, with a Backup for Microsoft 365 SQL injection to code execution and a Veeam ONE MFA bypass fixed the same day

Veeam published three advisories on 2026-10-27. In Backup & Replication, CVE-2026-108142 (CVSS 4.0 9.1, critical) lets an unauthenticated attacker bypass authorization on the CDP Coordinator Service of Windows-based Backup & Replication and of the Veeam Software Appliance; it affects 13.1.1.18 and all earlier 13.1 builds and 13.0.2.29 and all earlier 13.0 builds, is fixed in 13.1.2 (build 13.1.2.57) and 13.0.3 (build 13.0.3.63), and does not affect 12.x (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27). The same advisory fixes two medium path-traversal flaws that need the Restore Operator role plus control over the contents of a backed-up NAS share and that write attacker-controlled files to an arbitrary path on the backup server, and a local privilege escalation in Veeam Agent for Linux version 13.1.1.4 and earlier that applies only to agents managed by a Backup & Replication server (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27). Veeam Backup for Microsoft 365 8.5.0.1014 and earlier carry CVE-2026-106076 (9.0, critical): an authenticated organization-transfer peer injects SQL into the source server's configuration database, which gives cross-tenant read and write of configuration data and remote code execution as the PostgreSQL service account; the fix is 8.6 (build 8.6.0.1102), as it is for CVE-2026-106077 (8.3), which lets a user with the Backup for Microsoft 365 Administrator role read arbitrary files on the backup server as LocalSystem; two further flaws, an unauthenticated REST API authentication bypass with a forged federation token (6.9) and an installer file-write (4.3), need 8.6 Patch 1 (build 8.6.0.5011) (Veeam KB4957, 2026-10-27). Veeam ONE 13.1.0.7233 and earlier let an attacker with valid Administrator credentials disable multi-factor authentication globally before completing MFA verification (8.5, high; fixed in 13.1 P1, build 13.1.0.7940) (Veeam KB4951, 2026-10-27).

NCSC Switzerland relayed the Backup & Replication and Veeam ONE advisories on 2026-10-28, lists the exploitation status as unknown with the vendor reporting no evidence of active exploitation, and gives the prerequisite for the critical flaw as network access to the backup server's CDP Coordinator Service (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-28). heise adds that backup servers are a favourite target of ransomware groups (translated from German) (heise online, 2026-10-28), and Veeam itself says attackers will likely try to reverse-engineer a disclosed patch to exploit unpatched deployments (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
A Veeam Backup & Replication or Veeam Software Appliance on a 13.x build below 13.1.2 or 13.0.3 whose CDP Coordinator Service accepts connections from a network the attacker can reach; 12.x is out of scope (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27). Veeam Backup for Microsoft 365 version 8 below 8.6 Patch 1 (Veeam KB4957, 2026-10-27) and Veeam ONE 13.1 below Patch 1 (Veeam KB4951, 2026-10-27) are the other affected builds.
Detection
Veeam publishes no indicator. The telemetry that bears on this flaw is authentication and authorization events and service-account activity on the backup server, and new or changed backup jobs, repositories, stored credentials and restore operators; this is an inference from the described flaw, not a Veeam statement. For Veeam ONE, an MFA setting switched off followed by an Administrator sign-in is the sequence the flaw describes.
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed builds on every backup server first, since backup infrastructure is what ransomware groups try to reach before encrypting, and keep backup servers off networks that untrusted hosts can reach; where a backup server was reachable and unpatched, review its jobs, repositories and credentials for changes nobody made.

The earlier statement that no source ties a named CVE to a production compromise is replaced, an action for appliances that embed PHP is added, the URWB fix date in the vendor list is corrected from March 2027 to November 2026 (advisory version 1.9), and the PAN-OS hotfix status is updated to nineteen of twenty released (advisory of 2026-10-29). CISA's catalog entry of 2026-10-28 for the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 says it can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28). Dream Research reports a chain that takes these flaws to root on appliances: a custom, non-public PHP2Shell build for the management web server of one large vendor's firewall software, which runs PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit, gave code execution as the nobody user, and the kernel flaw lifted it to root in one HTTP request in under 15 minutes (Dream Research, 2026-10-27). Dream found the build tuned to eleven firmware versions, nine exploitable, with offsets from the vendor's own PHP library, the deployment-specific calibration CrowdStrike expects a reliable exploit to need (an inference) (Dream Research, 2026-10-27; CrowdStrike, 2026-10-23). From about 19,000 internet-facing firewalls of that vendor it narrowed to 240, rooted 24 and left a PHP webshell on each, and from the second of two firewalls of a US government-affiliated organization (the first crashed) built a persistent outbound SSH tunnel, rooted the organization's firewall management server through it and began an attack on its Active Directory; Dream could not tell whether that attack succeeded, does not name the vendor, calls the campaign apparently Chinese and AI-assisted and does not attribute it to a named actor (Dream Research, 2026-10-27). The targets were firewalls whose management interfaces were reachable from the internet (Dream Research, 2026-10-27).

Palo Alto Networks' advisory as read on 2026-10-29 lists all PAN-OS hotfixes as released except 11.1.7-h12, due on 2026-10-30 (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-29).
