item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-10-19
item.description: • Calendar-invite phishing spreads: Outlook and Gmail add the lure on their own and keep it after the email is deleted. Netcraft reports that phishing lures delivered as ICS calendar files, adopted by widespread campaigns of the EvilTokens Microsoft 365 token-stealing kit, are now spreading to low-effort scams. Outlook with Exchange Online (desktop, web and mobile) and Gmail with Google Calendar add such an invite to the calendar automatically as tentative and keep it after the email is deleted, so purging the message leaves the lure in place. EvilTokens invites posed as meetings, alerts or voicemail and led to a device-code page that has the victim authorise an attacker's device through OAuth; Sublime Security, quoted by The Guardian, reports exponential growth in calendar phishing. →
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01Calendar-invite phishing spreads: Outlook and Gmail add the lure on their own and keep it after the email is deleted. Netcraft reports that phishing lures delivered as ICS calendar files, adopted by widespread campaigns of the EvilTokens Microsoft 365 token-stealing kit, are now spreading to low-effort scams. Outlook with Exchange Online (desktop, web and mobile) and Gmail with Google Calendar add such an invite to the calendar automatically as tentative and keep it after the email is deleted, so purging the message leaves the lure in place. EvilTokens invites posed as meetings, alerts or voicemail and led to a device-code page that has the victim authorise an attacker's device through OAuth; Sublime Security, quoted by The Guardian, reports exponential growth in calendar phishing. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 1Updates to prior coverage 9Action items 10

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures1 item

NOTABLENATOB2

Phishing lures sent as ICS calendar invites land in Outlook and Gmail calendars without a click and stay after the email is deleted; EvilTokens used them for Microsoft 365 device-code phishing

Netcraft reports that attackers send phishing lures as ICS calendar files because the "text/calendar" type is treated as low risk by major email clients, and that the mail client's normal invite handling then places the lure in the victim's calendar with no user interaction, often keeping it there after the original email is deleted (Netcraft, 2026-10-16). In Netcraft's client table, Outlook desktop, Outlook on the web and Outlook Mobile with Exchange Online and Gmail with Google Calendar add the event automatically, mark it tentative and keep it after the email is deleted, Apple Calendar connected to Exchange Online often does the same, and Apple Mail with iCloud does not add it (Netcraft, 2026-10-16).

Campaigns using the EvilTokens toolkit, which steals Microsoft 365 tokens, used ICS invites disguised as meetings, alerts or voicemail notifications; the link leads to a page that gives the user a device code and tells them to enter it on Microsoft's device authorization page, which grants an attacker's device access to the account through OAuth (Netcraft, 2026-10-16). Netcraft now also sees smaller scams carrying ordinary phishing content inside ICS files (Netcraft, 2026-10-16). Sublime Security reports "exponential growth" in calendar phishing, with lures such as voicemail notices, payment receipts and renewal warnings that link to fake Microsoft, Google or PayPal logins or give a phone number, and Cofense says some senders use legitimate platforms such as Zoom to send the invitations, so filtering those platforms would also block real meetings (The Guardian, 2026-10-11).

Exposure
Users of Outlook with Exchange Online and of Gmail with Google Calendar, whose clients add external invites to the calendar on their own (Netcraft, 2026-10-16).
Detection
Netcraft names no telemetry; from the delivery path it describes, the traces are inbound external messages carrying a calendar part or ICS attachment in mail-flow logs, tentative events from external organizers the user never accepted in calendar audit logs, and, for the EvilTokens variant, a device-code sign-in to the account shortly after such an event (Netcraft, 2026-10-16). When responding to a reported phish of this kind, remove the calendar entry as well as the email, because the entry persists after the email is deleted (Netcraft, 2026-10-16).
Defender takeaway
Treat email-attached invites as part of the phishing attack surface: review whether the mail client settings add invites from outside the organization automatically for staff who do not expect them, and extend phishing guidance and purge procedures to calendar entries for those who do (Netcraft, 2026-10-16).

Correction19 Oct 2026 21:08 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditheadlinesourcesevidencebody

The headline no longer calls both zero-days default-configuration: CVE-2026-88772 needs DTLS, on by default only on VPN virtual servers. Only CVE-2026-88771 applies to every deployment in default configuration; CVE-2026-88772 needs DTLS, which is on by default only on VPN virtual servers, as described above, so the headline no longer calls both default-configuration. watchTowr shows the crash-log script searching the logs for two Pitboss packet-engine messages, "missed too many heartbeats" or "unexpectedly died", and says it can take up to 24 hours to run (watchTowr Labs, 2026-09-28). Citrix's instruction to customers who had already upgraded for CVE-2026-88771 through CVE-2026-88778 and meet the CVE-2026-88779 preconditions is to "upgrade your deployment again" (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-04); the quote now cites that report.

First published 2026-08-29 · open finding →

Correction19 Oct 2026 21:07 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditsummaryactionsbody

Corrects four statements: PaperCut says only that Emergency Patch Release 3 addresses two known regressions, not that Release 2 introduced them (the record of 2026-09-03 says it did); the web-log hunt now covers the LogonMessage route watchTowr documents and is cited; Huntress's 47% figure is dated to 28 August; and GreyNoise's twelve domain-admin victims are its count at last observation, not a final tally out of 395. The attacker-chosen Derby database name is removed from the detection text and the action as an indicator value.

Four statements above are corrected. PaperCut's bulletin says Emergency Patch Release 3 "addresses two known regressions", broken SAML login and support for legacy Microsoft SQL Server drivers for external card lookup, without saying Release 2 introduced them, as the update of 2026-09-03 stated (PaperCut Software, 2026-09-10). The web-log hunt now covers requests that put a non-administrative page such as LogonMessage in front of the ConfigEditor component, the route watchTowr documents, since PaperCut checks authorization only for that first page; the earlier pattern listed only Error, Exception and Home and missed it (watchTowr, 2026-10-09). Huntress's estimate that 47% of the installations it tracks run v23 or older dates from 28 August (Huntress, 2026-08-28). GreyNoise counts twelve victim organizations where domain admin was reached as of its last observation, not as a final tally out of the 395 (GreyNoise, 2026-09-09). The detection text and the second action now describe the Derby artifact as an in-memory database under an attacker-chosen name, without printing the name itself, which is an indicator value (Huntress, 2026-08-28).

Sources: PaperCut Software (vendor security bulletin) · Huntress · Rapid7 · CERT-FR (ANSSI) advisory CERTFR-2026-AVI-1095 · NCSC-NL advisory NCSC-2026-0334 · GreyNoise · CISA KEV · watchTowr Labs · PaperCut Software (September security bulletin) · Hunt.io · PaperCut Software (product documentation)
HIGHCVE-2026-25085 +22updatedNATOB2

Claroty Team82: 23 vulnerabilities in Copeland XWEB Pro supervisory refrigeration controllers chain to unauthenticated root RCE; a deterministic admin password derived from the device's own MAC address is one of THREE independent pre-auth paths

First published 2026-08-28 · open finding →

Correction19 Oct 2026 21:06 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditsummarysectorscvessourcesverificationsourcing_notebody

CISA's ICS advisory ICSA-26-057-10, which this entry said could not be located, lists all 23 identifiers: three missing ones are added (CVE-2026-3037, CVE-2026-22877, CVE-2026-20797), CVE-2026-21718 is typed as the authentication bypass both sources call it, the field-controller link and the register-map wording follow Claroty, the 'zero interaction' claim and the energy sector, which no source supports, are removed, the sourcing note records CISA's CWE for CVE-2026-21718, and the entry is now two-source.

CISA published an ICS advisory for these flaws on 2026-02-26, ICSA-26-057-10, contrary to the earlier statement that it could not be located; it lists all 23 identifiers with a summary and score each (CISA, 2026-02-26). The three not recorded before are CVE-2026-3037, an authenticated OS command injection through the MBird SMS service URL or code on the utility route (CVSS 8.0), so the authenticated command-injection flaws number eighteen, not seventeen; CVE-2026-22877, an arbitrary file read without authentication (CVSS 3.7); and CVE-2026-20797, a stack-based buffer overflow in an API route, reachable without authentication, that terminates the program (CVSS 4.3) (CISA, 2026-02-26). CVE-2026-21718 is an authentication bypass, as both Claroty and CISA call it, not a logic flaw (CISA, 2026-02-26).

Three descriptions above are corrected. The admin password is computed offline once the attacker has the MAC address and the date, which Claroty says can be obtained via unauthenticated public endpoints; the earlier "zero interaction with the target" overstated that (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09). The supervisory controller reaches its field controllers over an RS485 serial network using Modbus, and Ethernet is its own network connection, not a field-device link (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09). Claroty says the register addresses for many functions are not publicly documented and that it built the map from the XR60CX datasheet and protocol analysis (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09). The sectors now read retail and healthcare, which Claroty names through supermarkets, food distribution and healthcare facilities, in place of energy, which no source supports (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09); with CISA's advisory the flaws rest on two sources. The remediation is unchanged.

Not added: nginx-security-advisories (S1; a static list of flaws nginx.org itself rates medium, F5's own PSIRT relays are the corroboration) and infoblox-threat-intel (S3; this fire returned only dropped leads from it, commodity infrastructure research).

Coverage gaps: ibm-support-security-bulletins (no listing or feed transport reachable; IBM changes surface only through NCSC-NL relays), juniper support portal and hub.ivanti.com (JavaScript shells; the Junos data came from NCSC-NL's CSAF and CCCS), the ConnectWise remediation-guide PDF (403 on every transport; the Trust Center page carries the same workflow), the Politico body behind the ETS lead (navigation shell). WebSearch was not date-aware this weekend and returned mostly 2019 to 2025 material for Swiss incident queries; the curated feeds and authority listings were the effective discovery path.

Essential-coverage: all 21 essential records were attempted (S1 11, S2 10) and returned content; every authority feed was quiet.

Excluded as recent attempts: 0; the rotation cursor ranked the four slices (S1 14, S2 14, S3 14, S4 14 standard or candidate records) and the belt-and-braces exclusion removed none. S3's twelve extra major-lab listing sweeps and S4's Swiss and DACH leak-feed checks are in the sub-agent ledgers.

Self-identification: main agent Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) from the harness-injected model line; all four research sub-agents reported Sonnet 5.5 from their own prompt line.

Source health: tools/source_health.py probed 251 records and the first sweep put four on the UNSOLVED list, all fixed in this run and the second sweep ended with 250 relevant, one stale (threatpost, a demoted record) and no action: ox-security (the blog listing refuses every transport including WebFetch, the WordPress feed reads direct, so its recipe moved to the feed), nextjs-blog and cash-ch-awp (general-news scope: mostly non-security feeds), ncsc-ch-incidents (a low-cadence list at 61 days against a 60-day limit, max_staleness_days: 120).

Source-recipe notes (for the next audit): the Dixell France guide PDF cited by the Danfoss entry was replaced in place on 2026-10-18 (same file name, new content, Last-Modified 16:39 GMT) after the entry had quoted it, and check_run.py's quote-literal check cannot read PDFs, so a changed PDF is invisible to the gate; the audit's --page-checks-since pass is also blind to it. The ConnectWise Trust Center page is a living stack whose earlier dated blocks and FAQ are edited in place, so a statement about when something first appeared on it needs a dated update or an archive snapshot, never the current FAQ.

Verification: three iterations. Iteration 1 (NEEDS_FIXES, 5 truth, 2 editorial, 3 advisory) caught an error of mine, a claim that SaaS Security and Cloud Management were suspended since the advisory's first version, which rested on an undated FAQ block added later, plus a misstated token mechanism, two over-attributions and the Danfoss delta I had wrongly dropped. Iteration 2 (NEEDS_FIXES, 4 truth, 2 editorial, 2 advisory) found that the Dixell France PDF the Danfoss entry cites had been replaced on 2026-10-18, which turned that entry's record into a correction. Iteration 3 (NEEDS_FIXES, 2 truth, 0 editorial, 4 advisory) reported two low-confidence wording points and no F1 or F4, so the low-residual early exit applies (truth plus editorial of 2): the fixes were applied after the pass, five of the six findings, and one advisory was declined with its reason; no confirmation pass followed. This is an early-exit publish on a NEEDS_FIXES final verdict with verification_residual_count 2, and the two wording fixes were not independently re-read. After the pass the gate ended 56 pass, 0 warn, 0 fail apart from the run-clock stamp that Phase 6 re-stamps.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-10-18
item.description:
• ConnectWise SkyKick app credential used in 162+ Microsoft 365 tenants; disabling it does not undo planted access. ConnectWise says it identified unauthorized access to application identities of its Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) service; Huntress and Todyl report that from 15 October the app's credential was used to obtain app-only Microsoft Graph tokens in customer Microsoft 365 tenants; Huntress alone confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants by 16 October and saw ConnectWise Cloud Management apps assign themselves directory roles in about 50 tenants and, in two tenants, a scripted Global Administrator self-grant followed by new client secrets planted on apparently random applications. ConnectWise disabled seven application identities and suspended the service on 17 October, but says disabling does not reverse changes already made in a tenant, so every tenant that ever consented a ConnectWise or SkyKick app needs the apps disabled and its application credentials, directory roles and consents reviewed. Microsoft assesses that the China-state aligned actor Storm-0940 is behind it, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework, and says it attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants; how the credential was obtained and what data was read are not public. →
  • Some Rank Math PRO 3.0.123 downloads carried malware; updating to 3.0.124 does not remove what it left. Rank Math says some copies of its WordPress plugin Rank Math PRO 3.0.123, downloaded or updated between 2026-10-15 20:02 UTC and 2026-10-16 07:12 UTC, contained malware that could compromise a site once the plugin is activated, and it released 3.0.124 as the clean build. The malware can recreate a hidden backdoor on page visits and may leave administrator accounts, scheduled tasks and files outside the plugin, so an affected site needs the plugin folder and persistence removed in a set order, a restore or cleanup, and rotation of every credential the site could reach; how the vendor's distribution was compromised and who is behind it are not disclosed. →
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01ConnectWise SkyKick app credential used in 162+ Microsoft 365 tenants; disabling it does not undo planted access. ConnectWise says it identified unauthorized access to application identities of its Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) service; Huntress and Todyl report that from 15 October the app's credential was used to obtain app-only Microsoft Graph tokens in customer Microsoft 365 tenants; Huntress alone confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants by 16 October and saw ConnectWise Cloud Management apps assign themselves directory roles in about 50 tenants and, in two tenants, a scripted Global Administrator self-grant followed by new client secrets planted on apparently random applications. ConnectWise disabled seven application identities and suspended the service on 17 October, but says disabling does not reverse changes already made in a tenant, so every tenant that ever consented a ConnectWise or SkyKick app needs the apps disabled and its application credentials, directory roles and consents reviewed. Microsoft assesses that the China-state aligned actor Storm-0940 is behind it, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework, and says it attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants; how the credential was obtained and what data was read are not public. →
  2. 02Some Rank Math PRO 3.0.123 downloads carried malware; updating to 3.0.124 does not remove what it left. Rank Math says some copies of its WordPress plugin Rank Math PRO 3.0.123, downloaded or updated between 2026-10-15 20:02 UTC and 2026-10-16 07:12 UTC, contained malware that could compromise a site once the plugin is activated, and it released 3.0.124 as the clean build. The malware can recreate a hidden backdoor on page visits and may leave administrator accounts, scheduled tasks and files outside the plugin, so an affected site needs the plugin folder and persistence removed in a set order, a restore or cleanup, and rotation of every credential the site could reach; how the vendor's distribution was compromised and who is behind it are not disclosed. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 2Updates to prior coverage 5Action items 11

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures2 items

HIGHexploitedupdatedNATOA1

ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick): the vendor's Microsoft 365 application credential was used to sign in to customer tenants, with directory-role self-assignments in about 50 tenants and, Huntress reports, added credentials in two

ConnectWise says it identified unauthorized access to application identities within its Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) environment; on 2026-10-17 it disabled seven application identities, suspended the service, says the shared Cloud Backup credentials are no longer valid, and warns that disabling does not reverse changes already made in a tenant (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). As of ConnectWise's update of 2026-10-19 01:15 UTC, Cloud Backup, SaaS Security and Cloud Management remained suspended with no confirmed restoration time (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19), and its status page of 2026-10-28 says partners can now re-authorize Microsoft 365 backup and restore through a new application (ConnectWise status page, 2026-10-28); ConnectWise reports no successful threat activity in the environments it monitors since it implemented mitigations (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19) and says it cannot independently determine whether a given partner or customer tenant was affected (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Huntress and Todyl report that on 2026-10-15 the app's identity signed in to customer Microsoft 365 tenants from one hosting-provider address and received app-only Microsoft Graph tokens; the credential sits in the vendor's own tenant, so no user, MFA prompt or user Conditional Access was involved, and the app's consent covers read and write access to mail, files and Teams chats (Huntress, 2026-10-16; Todyl, 2026-10-15). Huntress confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants by 2026-10-16 and later counted almost 1,000 tenants with sign-in activity from that address, over 300 successful, after password spraying against four law-firm tenants on 13 and 14 October, and a separate failed wave targeted 16 tenants in policy and national-security sectors (Huntress, 2026-10-16). In about 50 of its tenants, ConnectWise Cloud Management apps assigned themselves directory roles, mostly Exchange Administrator; in one the Teams app added itself to Global Administrator and client secrets were added to an MSP management application and to Huntress's own application within about five minutes, the credential additions from private Azure space (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Huntress later identified a second tenant with the same sequence, the application granting itself Global Administrator and then planting a new secret on a small number of other applications, within two minutes of the first around 03:45 UTC on 2026-10-15, with the choice of applications apparently random (Huntress, 2026-10-16). It says the unauthorized sign-ins with the credential were bunched across the morning of 2026-10-15 UTC, that the last successful one it observed was at 08:44 UTC that day with only failed attempts afterwards in the tenants where it can read sign-in logs, and that in the two tenants it reviewed it found no mailbox or file manipulation and no user or policy changes (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Microsoft Threat Intelligence, as BleepingComputer relays it, called it an active supply-chain attack and assessed likely abuse of existing permissions including Directory.ReadWrite.All (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-17). Microsoft Threat Intelligence later assessed that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, was responsible, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). How the credential was obtained and what was read remain unknown (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-17).

Exposure
Every Entra tenant, including each customer tenant an MSP manages, in which a ConnectWise or SkyKick Cloud Backup or Cloud Management app was ever consented, dormant connections included; ConnectWise lists seven application client IDs, among them Cloud Backup (506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), and says to match on client ID (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Todyl identifies the application as "ConnectWise Cloud Backup" (formerly SkyKick Backup), app ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae; SpecterOps hunts for applications owned by the ConnectWise tenant (ID 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7) and notes that older tenants may list them under SkyKick names (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17).
Detection
Entra service-principal sign-in logs for these apps from any address outside Microsoft and Azure ranges, which misses the credential additions, made from private Azure space (Huntress, 2026-10-16); the sweep of sign-ins itself, which Sophos saw come from a single virtual private server in strictly ascending tenant-ID order with Python HTTP-library user agents (Sophos, 2026-10-19); directory audit events Add member to role, Update application and Add service principal credentials initiated by a ConnectWise or SkyKick app (Huntress, 2026-10-16); Graph activity logs (Entra ID P1 or P2, not retroactive) for per-request source addresses (Todyl, 2026-10-15); and mailbox forwarding, inbox and transport rule and delegation changes (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Huntress notes that Microsoft Graph directory reads leave no audit record, so a clean audit log does not rule out reads of the directory (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Disabling the apps does not remove credentials, roles or consents already planted, and revoking user sessions does not end this access (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19; Todyl, 2026-10-15). Disabling an app stops new tokens only: a token issued before the disable stays valid for up to 90 minutes (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17), and ConnectWise says that after its own certificate revocation previously issued tokens may remain usable until they expire (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). The service-principal sign-in log records an application's authentication (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19), while per-request use of a token appears in the Graph activity logs named above (Todyl, 2026-10-15), so the review of that period belongs there. Microsoft asks tenants to review service-principal sign-ins from at least 2026-10-15, and from 2026-10-01 where records exist, and to search by application ID rather than display name (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). As of 2026-10-19, any alerting a tenant took from ConnectWise SaaS Security was out of service while that service was suspended (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19).

Triage: the vendor's apps sign in from Azure addresses with a .NET SDK user agent, while the credential additions used a Python user agent; Python and curl are common in administration, so Huntress says the combination of actor, operation and user agent is the signal (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Role self-assignments carrying the vendor's own user agent are not proven benign, since Huntress has not confirmed vendor automation (Huntress, 2026-10-16).

Defender takeaway
Where any ConnectWise or SkyKick app is consented, disable it by client ID without deleting it, keep it disabled (ConnectWise's restoration works through a new application that each tenant consents separately), and review credentials, roles, owners, consents and Conditional Access exclusions since 13 October (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19; Huntress, 2026-10-16). An MSP should review its own management and security tools first, since a foothold there can reach its customers, but the review covers every application, because Huntress saw secrets planted on apparently random ones (Huntress, 2026-10-16). ConnectWise cannot independently determine whether a given partner or customer tenant was affected, so the answer for a tenant has to come from its own sign-in and audit logs (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19).
Improvement19 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-19T0256Z-intelactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

ConnectWise's update of 2026-10-18 01:00 UTC took SaaS Security and Cloud Management offline in addition to Cloud Backup, which had been suspended since 2026-10-17, so ConnectWise SaaS Security monitoring and alerting is out of service as well, and the update of 2026-10-19 01:15 UTC still gives no restoration time (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Disabling an app stops new tokens only: Todyl and SpecterOps each state that tokens already issued stay valid for up to 90 minutes, and ConnectWise says that after it revoked the Cloud Backup certificates previously issued tokens may remain usable until they expire (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17; ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). SpecterOps hunts for applications owned by the ConnectWise tenant, noting that older tenants may list them under SkyKick names (SpecterOps, 2026-10-17).

Update20 Oct 2026 03:57 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0256Z-inteltitlesummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Huntress's update of 2026-10-19 13:30 ET identified a second tenant with post-compromise activity, a tenant Huntress did not originally protect, where it got deployed to collect telemetry (Huntress, 2026-10-16). In both tenants the activity was fast and scripted, within two minutes of each other around 03:45 UTC on 2026-10-15: the application granted itself Global Administrator and then planted a new secret on a small number of other applications to keep a foothold (Huntress, 2026-10-16). The choice of applications appeared random: the same flow picked two different sets, one application present in both was backdoored in only one, and in one tenant the applications that received secrets were among the least privileged in the environment while far more powerful ones were untouched (Huntress, 2026-10-16).

Huntress says the unauthorized sign-ins with the credential were tightly bunched across the morning of 2026-10-15 UTC, the last confirmed successful sign-in it observed was at 08:44 UTC, and it saw only failed attempts afterwards in the tenants where it can read sign-in logs (Huntress, 2026-10-16). The access may have been used for Microsoft Graph directory reads, which leave no audit record, and in the two tenants Huntress reviewed it found no evidence of mailbox or file manipulation or of user or policy changes (Huntress, 2026-10-16). The check for planted credentials therefore has to cover every application registration and enterprise application in the tenant, and a clean audit log does not exclude directory reads. ConnectWise's latest readable update (2026-10-19 01:15 UTC) gives no restoration time (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19).

Improvement21 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0256Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Sophos X-Ops independently observed the token requests: on 2026-10-15 a single virtual private server authenticated as the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application and requested app-only Microsoft Graph tokens for about 96 minutes, from 07:11 UTC, in strictly ascending tenant-ID order, one to six minutes apart, using Python HTTP-library user agents, and the sweep included tenants with no active backup subscription (Sophos X-Ops, 2026-10-19). Sophos found no hands-on-keyboard activity and no evidence that the application created new secrets, applications, consents or role assignments in the tenants it reviewed, which differs from the role grants and added secrets Huntress reports in other tenants; Sophos says it is unclear how the credential was obtained and what was done with the tokens (Sophos X-Ops, 2026-10-19). The two vendors' sweep timings differ: Huntress puts the first app sign-ins at 06:13 to 08:34 UTC on 2026-10-15 with tenants taken in sorted GUID order a few seconds apart (Huntress, 2026-10-16), where Sophos gives about 96 minutes from 07:11 UTC, one to six minutes apart; the vantage points differ, so both are reported as stated.

Update22 Oct 2026 03:46 UTCrun 2026-10-22T0256Z-intelbodyentitiesevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, was responsible for the compromise. It says AI agents running the ARTEX framework kept signing in to customer tenants as the ConnectWise applications, without an interactive user sign-in, and in multiple tenants went on to Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to change privileges (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). It counts attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants and links the activity to an automated cross-tenant password spray between 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-14 against 327 accounts at eight organizations, from the same network range and including an address that ConnectWise's advisory later listed among its indicators; the spray peaked on 2026-10-11 at 2,900 failed logons a minute and produced no successful authentication (Microsoft, 2026-10-21).

Microsoft warns that the application credential changes can remain active as a backdoor after the vendor application is remediated, and asks tenants to review service-principal sign-ins from at least 2026-10-15, and from 2026-10-01 where records exist, together with the Entra audit trail for credential additions, role assignments, consents and owner changes (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Expel, which analysed the activity separately, relays the attribution, notes that ConnectWise's fix leaves secrets planted on other applications in place and that Graph directory reads leave no Entra audit record, and says Huntress has not tied its Global Administrator observation to the same operator (Expel, 2026-10-21). ConnectWise itself says that, based on the evidence available to it, including threat intelligence shared by Microsoft, it appears a China state-aligned group was responsible and used an openly available agentic AI framework (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21). It began restoring services in controlled phases on 2026-10-21, expects it to take several days, says the start of restoration does not mean all capabilities are available, and tells partners to keep affected connections disabled until formal instructions apply to their service, while noting that its actions do not remove unauthorized access already established in individual customer tenants (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21; heise online, 2026-10-21).

Correction25 Oct 2026 13:43 UTCrun 2026-10-25T1308Z-auditbodyevidence

The update of 2026-10-22 attached a rate of 2,900 attempts a minute to the ARTEX sign-ins against more than 2,250 tenants. Microsoft gives no rate for those sign-ins: 2,900 a minute is the peak of failed logons in the separate password spray of 10 to 14 October, reached on 11 October (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). The figure now sits with the spray.

Improvement27 Oct 2026 03:46 UTCrun 2026-10-27T0256Z-intelevidencesourcessourcing_note

Huntress published its analysis of what drove the 2026-10-15 activity on 2026-10-26, working from Entra sign-in and directory audit logs in the tenants it monitors. It says its telemetry aligns with Microsoft's Storm-0940 and ARTEX account without independently confirming it, that it is highly confident an operator, a person or an LLM, adapted the tooling between runs, and that its confidence that an LLM was involved in the escalation tooling is low to medium on its own telemetry and medium to high once Microsoft's attribution is included (Huntress, 2026-10-26). Its evidence for adaptation: a certificate upload that failed on a thumbprint mismatch ended one run with no retry, and the next run 55 seconds later retried the same error with growing waits until it worked; in a second tenant that refused removal of the Global Administrator role, the actor granted a different role to a sibling principal and the original service principal was then deleted (Huntress, 2026-10-26). Microsoft Graph reads are not recorded in the Entra audit log and no victim Huntress knows of had Graph activity logging enabled, so a clean audit log does not show that no Graph access took place (Huntress, 2026-10-26). Huntress recommends alerting when a service principal assigns itself Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator, deletes itself, or when one vendor principal grants a role to a sibling, and turning on Graph activity logs where licensing allows (Huntress, 2026-10-26).

Update29 Oct 2026 04:59 UTCrun 2026-10-29T0255Z-intelupdated_atsourcesevidenceactionsbody

ConnectWise's status page announced on 2026-10-28 at 17:09 UTC, after restoration in controlled phases had begun on 2026-10-21, that it is beginning phased restoration for partners, starting with Microsoft 365 backups and restores through a new, security-hardened application, with other features returning in phases over the coming days (ConnectWise status page, 2026-10-28). Partners must re-authorize each Microsoft 365 tenant using the new application, “ConnectWise Cloud Backup for M365”, to resume backup and restore operations, and ConnectWise points to its Trust Center for the detailed instructions (ConnectWise status page, 2026-10-28). Before that, from 2026-10-26, it had said it would first enable a process to restore data from existing backups and then phased re-enrollment, and it still told partners to keep affected connections disabled until instructions applied to their service (ConnectWise status page, 2026-10-28).

incident18 Oct 03:30Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: ConnectWise Trust Center (advisory) · Huntress · Todyl · BleepingComputer · SpecterOps · Sophos X-Ops · Microsoft Threat Intelligence · Expel · heise online · Huntress (AI, Scripts, Operator: Inside the ConnectWise Attack) · ConnectWise status page (Cloud Backup incident, update of 2026-10-28 17:09 UTC)
NOTABLECVE-2026-111862updatedNATOA2

Rank Math SEO PRO 3.0.123: some packages served for about eleven hours carried malware that can leave hidden backdoors, rogue administrators and cron persistence that the update to 3.0.124 does not remove

Rank Math says that some copies of Rank Math PRO 3.0.123, downloaded between 2026-10-15 20:02 UTC and 2026-10-16 07:12 UTC, contained malware that could compromise a website if the plugin was activated, and that it removed the files and released 3.0.124 (Rank Math, 2026-10-16). It says the malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits the website, so removing suspicious files before disabling the mechanism that recreates them may not resolve the infection (Rank Math, 2026-10-16). Wordfence adds that the malware may establish persistent access, contact a remote host, and expose WordPress credentials, database credentials, API keys and other secrets that the web server can reach, and that Rank Math says it holds records of who downloaded an affected copy (Wordfence, 2026-10-17). The signs Rank Math lists are three malicious entries in the WordPress options table, hidden PHP backdoors in the must-use plugins directory and in other plugin and theme folders, unknown administrator accounts, a fake core file under wp-includes, .htaccess rules that let .cache files run as PHP, PHP files in the uploads directory and a web-user cron entry carrying a marker comment (Rank Math, 2026-10-16).

Exposure
A site that downloaded or updated Rank Math PRO 3.0.123 inside the stated window; Rank Math says the installed version shows under Plugins (Rank Math, 2026-10-16), and Wordfence stresses that 3.0.123 alone does not establish compromise (Wordfence, 2026-10-17). Rank Math says a copy installed and activated in the window means a compromised site, a copy installed but never activated means deleting the files, installing 3.0.124 and scanning, and a copy only downloaded shows no sign of compromise from this incident alone (Rank Math, 2026-10-16).
Detection
The web-server user's crontab and the WordPress scheduled events, the list of administrator accounts, WordPress core integrity (wp core verify-checksums), PHP files under the must-use plugins and uploads directories and in other plugins and themes, and web-server egress to the host Rank Math names (Rank Math, 2026-10-16). Rank Math also says the attacker may have changed things outside the WordPress directory, so review SSH authorized_keys files and other users' crontabs (Rank Math, 2026-10-16). Post-patch compromise check: updating replaces the affected package but does not remove files, accounts or scheduled tasks the malware already created elsewhere (Wordfence, 2026-10-17).
Defender takeaway
Treat a site that activated an affected copy as compromised: restore from a backup older than 2026-10-15 20:02 UTC, or, if cleaning by hand, delete the whole plugin folder (deactivating is not enough), remove the malicious options and block the malicious host Rank Math names before anything else, then clean the rest; either way rotate the WordPress, database, API, hosting and SSH credentials the site could reach, and install 3.0.124 only from the vendor's own account page, since Rank Math says it sends no login or download links by email (Rank Math, 2026-10-16).
Improvement19 Oct 2026 21:04 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditcvessourcesbody

Wordfence has assigned the malicious 3.0.123 packages the identifier CVE-2026-111862, recorded as embedded malicious code with a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, affected version 3.0.123 and patched version 3.0.124 (Wordfence Intelligence, 2026-10-16), so vulnerability scanners and tickets keyed on the identifier match this incident. The record, like Rank Math, limits the affected packages to those obtained during the stated window and says version 3.0.123 alone does not establish compromise (Wordfence Intelligence, 2026-10-16).

incident18 Oct 03:31Zsingle-source · victim disclosureOpen finding →
Sources: Rank Math · Wordfence · Wordfence Intelligence

02Updates to prior coverage5 items

ROUTINECVE-2026-84411updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-84411, MikroTik RouterOS: one unauthenticated request to the web management service can run code as root; fixed in 7.24 (v7 stable), 7.23.8 (v7 long-term) and 6.49.23 (v6 long-term) (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

First published 2026-10-10 · open finding →

Correction18 Oct 2026 13:59 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditevidencebody

The quotation of the RouterOS 7.23.8 changelog line is corrected to its exact text, which names a second CVE, CVE-2026-103903, beside CVE-2026-84411; only the 6.49.23 release carries the line with CVE-2026-84411 alone.

The correction of 2026-10-13 quoted both long-term changelogs as listing the same line. Only RouterOS 6.49.23 reads "system - improve stability (includes CVE-2026-84411);" (MikroTik forum, 2026-10-09). The RouterOS 7.23.8 changelog reads "system - improve stability (includes CVE-2026-84411, CVE-2026-103903);", so 7.23.8 also fixes a second flaw, CVE-2026-103903, that MikroTik's changelog names without describing (MikroTik, 2026-10-08). The upgrade advice is unchanged.

Sources: MikroTik (security notice) · MikroTik (RouterOS 7.23.8 changelog) · MikroTik forum (6.49.23 long-term release announcement) · MikroTik forum (7.23.8 long-term release announcement) · CISA (ICSA-26-272-06) · BleepingComputer · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog
HIGHCVE-2026-102255 +3updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-102255, SonicWall SMA1000: a third unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 Work Place SSRF this year, affecting the hotfix builds that closed the September zero-days, with exploitation attempts reported that SonicWall has not confirmed

First published 2026-10-08 · open finding →

Correction18 Oct 2026 13:59 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditbody

The 2026-10-10 update attributed a count of 135 attempts from two addresses between 9 and 10 October to Previdian's page. The page carries no such window: the 135 attempts from two US addresses is the count The Hacker News relayed on 2026-10-12, and Previdian's page now shows 1,887 attempts from five addresses between 9 and 16 October.

The update of 2026-10-10 said Previdian's page counted 135 attempts from two source addresses between 9 and 10 October. Previdian's page gives no such window. The figure of 135 attempts from two unique US addresses is the count The Hacker News relayed "to date" on 2026-10-12 (The Hacker News, 2026-10-12). Read on 2026-10-18, Previdian's page records 1,887 attempts from five addresses in Singapore and the United States, first observed on 9 October and last on 16 October (Previdian, 2026-10-12).

CVE-2026-88771 / CVE-2026-88772, Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway: unauthenticated pre-auth RCE zero-days exploited before a patch existed (CVSS 4.0 9.5)

First published 2026-09-28 · open finding →

Improvement18 Oct 2026 03:35 UTCrun 2026-10-18T0256Z-intelentitiesreferencesactionssourcesevidencebody

Zscaler ThreatLabz's first-party exploitation telemetry (2026-10-16) adds post-exploitation behaviour to the compromise check: a Perl CGI handler enabled in the web server configuration besides PHP, and a variant that makes the appliance download and run a 64-bit FreeBSD binary, seen in a burst from at least 26 source addresses; the download server also appeared in its earlier Magento exploitation data, which ThreatLabz calls a lead and not attribution.

Zscaler ThreatLabz published first-party telemetry of exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 on 2026-10-16 (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16). The chain it captured matches the log-poisoning sequence in the sections above: a payload stored in the User-Agent of GET requests to four default logon and VPN paths, a forged packet-engine failure record in the authentication request that searches the access log for the marker, decodes the payload and runs it when the vendor's crash-log script selects that record (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16). Two post-exploitation behaviours are not described above: the payload writes PHP and Perl CGI web shells into six web-served directories and adds a handler that runs .pl files as CGI, besides switching PHP on in the web server configuration, and a shorter variant makes the appliance download a Rust-built 64-bit FreeBSD binary and run it from /var (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16). ThreatLabz saw at least 26 source addresses send the forged record together with that downloader within about six to seven minutes (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16). It says the download server also appeared in its earlier exploitation data for CVE-2026-75650, the Adobe Commerce and Magento flaw it tracks as StyleSmuggler, and calls the overlap an investigative lead that does not establish attribution, because shared hosting, a malware-distribution service or payload reuse by unrelated operators could explain it (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16).

CVE-2026-105133 / CVE-2026-105134, AhsayCBS backup management console: an unauthenticated authentication-bypass and code-execution chain exploited since 7 October to drop webshells and a cryptominer; Ahsay says its earlier patches were incomplete and ships hotfixes 10.3.4.45 and 9.15.2.70 through its partner portal

First published 2026-10-10 · open finding →

Improvement18 Oct 2026 03:34 UTCrun 2026-10-18T0256Z-intelsourcesevidenceactionsbody

Horizon3.ai's source-level analysis of 2026-10-14 gives the root cause of both flaws (a caller-set flag that skips the administrator credential check, and an upload path that escapes the folder denylist), shows the chain runs as root on Linux, and lists server-side hunt artifacts: new .jsp files in served application directories, replication receivers created outside a change window, unexpected system administrator accounts, and requests carrying the bypass field or the receiver upload headers.

Horizon3.ai published a source-level analysis of both flaws on 2026-10-14, working from the Linux installer, and says its proof of concept for the chain, from authentication bypass to a webshell, is on its GitHub (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). For CVE-2026-105133, every action of the JSON API extends a base class whose administrator password check is skipped when the request body carries a FromServlet flag that the caller sets, so the JSON API is reachable without credentials, and the AddSysUser action, which creates a system administrator, never consults the caller (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). For CVE-2026-105134, an authentication-bypassed call creates a replication receiver whose home directory the attacker chooses; the system-folder denylist that screens that directory at creation is not applied to the upload path later built from two attacker-supplied headers, in which only the percent and colon characters are escaped, so a traversal sequence walks the write location into a served web application, and one upload of a .jsp file then runs as LocalSystem on Windows and as root on Linux (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). Horizon3 says Ahsay released its hotfixes on 12 October 2026 (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14).

Sources: Huntress · BleepingComputer · SecurityWeek · Ahsay (AhsayCBS 10.3.4 release notes) · Ahsay (security alert update) · Bitdefender · CISA · Horizon3.ai

Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised, with forced defrost reported at hundreds of French supermarkets; CERT-FR and NCSC Switzerland say to remove internet exposure

First published 2026-10-13 · open finding →

Update18 Oct 2026 03:33 UTCrun 2026-10-18T0256Z-intelsummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

CERT-FR's alert has a third version dated 2026-10-16 whose guidance differs for compromised and uncompromised units: the whole configuration, defrost ranges included, is to be checked, and a compromised Danfoss unit is to be restarted or otherwise factory-reset and reconfigured, with a caution to check insurance conditions before cutting the contractor's data uplink. The Dixell France operator guide that the alert links says any XWEB PRO on firmware 1.12.1 or earlier must be updated without delay, that XWEB units ship with a factory Admin account, and that remote access must go through an encrypted VPN; neither document names an entry vector.

CERT-FR's alert now has a third version, dated 2026-10-16 and listed on the page as an update of the recommendations; the page does not show which sentences changed (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). Its current text separates the two cases. For every unit it asks to remove the internet exposure of the affected units and of any unit on a public IP address, and to check the insurance contract conditions before cutting the data uplink to the refrigeration contractor (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). For a unit not known to be compromised it then asks to check the whole configuration, notably the defrost ranges; for a compromised Danfoss unit it says to restart the equipment or otherwise restore it with a factory reset, and then to reconfigure it for service (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). In both cases access returns only through a secure VPN or protected network, with source-address filtering for the contractors an emergency measure and not a lasting one, and the maker's practices apply (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). The alert still says campaigns are probably ongoing, still names no flaw or entry vector, and gives the risk as not specified by the vendor (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16).

The alert's documentation section links an operator guide from Dixell France (Copeland) (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). The file at that address was replaced on 2026-10-18; its current text, described in the correction of 2026-10-19T04:06:00Z, is Copeland's bulletin of 14 October 2026 followed by Dixell France's own complement (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). That complement says XWEB PRO and EVO ship with the same factory account, Admin with the password Admin, advises keeping the original Admin password sealed or in a password manager and not using it daily, gives each user a named account with an expiry date for an external contractor's account, and requires remote access through an encrypted VPN, with no port forward or DMZ and no remote-control software such as AnyDesk or TeamViewer on a site PC that stays on (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). CERT-FR does not say how the attackers got in, and SecurityWeek writes that neither Danfoss nor French authorities have tied the attack to the flaws Claroty disclosed (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16; SecurityWeek, 2026-10-15).

Sources: CERT-FR (alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012) · AFP · BFMTV · Infosecurity Magazine · BleepingComputer · CERT-FR (alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012, revised version) · NCSC Switzerland (Security Hub advisory 13054) · Cooling Post · Blick · Censys · CERT-FR (alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012, third version) · Dixell France (Copeland) · Le Monde · SecurityWeek · Cybersecurity Dive · Public Sénat · Le Monde Informatique · Forescout Research (Vedere Labs)

03Action items11 items

  • Upgrade every internet-facing NetScaler ADC/Gateway to 14.1-73.37+ (14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.37 FIPS+) or 13.1-64.23+ (13.1-FIPS/NDcPP 13.1-37.279+) now (a SAML-configured appliance needs the later builds named for CVE-2026-88779, and an identity provider 14.1-73.46 or 13.1-64.29); on a 13.1-branch appliance run show ns variable first; if it returns any variables, install 13.1-64.24 instead to avoid a known reboot loop. Capture logs, an instance snapshot where the appliance is virtual, a support bundle and a core dump from each exposed appliance BEFORE patching, since the upgrade can remove forensic evidence of prior exploitation.
    FindingCVE-2026-88771 +7→
  • Run Mandiant's compromise checks, extended by the Unit 42 artifacts described in the update below, Zscaler's (appliance-initiated downloads to unfamiliar addresses, an unexpected executable under /var, a Perl CGI handler added to the web server configuration) and Rapid7's (the setuid bit on /bin/sh, nsaaad crashes followed by Pitboss reboots, an outbound agent polling an external endpoint every 15 seconds), on every NetScaler that was internet-facing and unpatched at any time since early September, patched or not; isolate any hit, check both nodes of an HA pair, halt HA configuration sync until both nodes are validated, and rotate the LDAP and RADIUS bind credentials, SSL private keys and key-encryption material held in the configuration, since Rapid7 saw the configuration and backups staged and exfiltrated.
    FindingCVE-2026-88771 +7→
  • Find any NetScaler ADC or Gateway still on the end-of-life 12.1 or 13.0 branches and decide isolation or replacement now: they receive no security updates and Citrix has not said whether they are affected.
    FindingCVE-2026-88771 +7→
  • Find every Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controller in facilities you own or that a contractor manages for you and take its management interface off the internet now, restoring access only through a secure VPN or protected network (filtering to the contractor's source addresses is an emergency stop-gap, and CERT-FR asks you to check your insurance conditions before cutting the contractor's data uplink); an end-of-life unit that gets no fixes needs replacing, because a factory reset leaves it vulnerable and probably compromised again.
    FindingANSSI says the refrigeration attacks used exposure…→
  • On every such controller that was reachable from the internet, check the whole configuration, defrost ranges included, against the intended one; for a Danfoss unit that may have been taken over, restart it or otherwise factory-reset it, restore access only through a secure VPN or protected network and reconfigure it for service, then update its firmware, set the security level to Strict and replace the default and any weak passwords, and on every Copeland or Dixell XWEB unit confirm the factory Admin password was changed and give each contractor a named account with an expiry date.
    FindingANSSI says the refrigeration attacks used exposure…→
  • In every Entra tenant you or your MSP administer, disable without deleting the seven ConnectWise application identities that ConnectWise lists by client ID (Cloud Backup is 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae; the other six are in ConnectWise's advisory), dormant connections included, and keep them disabled, because ConnectWise's restoration of 2026-10-28 has partners consent a new application, “ConnectWise Cloud Backup for M365”, in each tenant, so take its details only from the instructions on ConnectWise's Trust Center; where Graph activity logs were enabled, review them for these apps until at least 90 minutes after you disabled them, because a token issued before the disable stays valid for up to 90 minutes, and preserve the sign-in and audit logs promptly without delaying containment, because Entra ID Free keeps only 7 days.
    FindingConnectWise SkyKick app credential used in 162+…→
  • In the same tenants list the apps owned by the ConnectWise tenant (ID 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7), and disable each that you do not use or cannot verify as safe.
    FindingConnectWise SkyKick app credential used in 162+…→
  • In the same tenants review every enterprise application and app registration, MSP management and security tools first but none skipped (Huntress saw the secrets planted on apparently random applications, in one tenant on some of the least privileged ones), for client secrets, certificates and federated credentials added since 2026-10-13 and remove any you did not create; also check the directory roles, owners and consent grants held by ConnectWise and SkyKick service principals, Conditional Access exclusions for them, and mailbox forwarding, inbox and transport rules and delegated access, because disabling the vendor applications does not remove access planted through them.
    FindingConnectWise SkyKick app credential used in 162+…→
  • Find every AhsayCBS server your organisation or your managed-service suppliers run, including those already on v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59, and apply the hotfix v10.3.4.45 (v10) or v9.15.2.70 (v7, v8, v9) now, then reboot it; the hotfixes sit behind Ahsay's partner portal, so ask the integrator or Ahsay for the build, and until it is applied keep the management web interface behind a VPN or an allowlist of trusted addresses.
    FindingCVE-2026-105133 +1→
  • Compromise-check every AhsayCBS server that was internet-reachable since 2026-10-04 against the indicators Huntress and Bitdefender publish, an OpenSSH service nobody installed included, and against Horizon3's server-side checks (new .jsp files in served application directories, replication receivers created outside a change window, unexpected system administrator accounts), and re-image any host with a confirmed compromise from a trusted backup, because the hotfix does not remove a webshell or a persistence mechanism that is already there.
    FindingCVE-2026-105133 +1→
  • Find every WordPress site that your organisation, its web agencies or its hosting suppliers run with Rank Math PRO and establish whether 3.0.123 was downloaded or updated between 2026-10-15 20:02 UTC and 2026-10-16 07:12 UTC; on a site where it was activated, restore from a backup older than that window or, if cleaning by hand, delete the whole rank-math-pro folder and the malicious database options first, because the backdoor is rebuilt on page visits, and rotate every credential the site could reach.
    FindingCVE-2026-111862→
Verification & coverage notes2 runs

2026-10-18T1307Z-audit · audit · Opus 5.5 · window 168 h · 1 entry published

Verification & coverage notes

Scheduled quality audit over the trailing week, 2026-10-11T13:07Z to 2026-10-18T13:07Z, anchored on the 2026-10-11 audit. The fire started under v4.19 with a window back to 2026-09-30 and the legacy queue, stopped on the API rate limit, and on resumption was re-based on main under v4.21 (base 74695f56, claim pushed first) and cut to the week, as the operator directed. Report: docs/audits/2026-10-18-quality-audit.md.

Soundness. The week's 30 entries (21 filed by the fires, 9 older entries they updated) were truth-passed in T1, T2, T3, T6b and T9, minus NeedyMantis, which the 2026-10-11 audit's loop verified. 16 of 29 clean, 9 with imprecisions only, 4 with factual errors (Bricksforge's fixed versions, PaperCut's Release 3 regressions, SonicWall's Previdian count, MikroTik's 7.23.8 changelog line); a cited-page check added the Exchange entry's stale banner quotes. Every defect is fixed through a changelog record: one update (Bricksforge), five reader-facing corrections (Copeland, PaperCut, Citrix, SonicWall, MikroTik), one reader-facing improvement (Rank Math's CVE-2026-111862), and internal records for metadata (Ivanti, BeyondTrust, PeerStitch, AhsayCBS, Publica, Danfoss, Exchange, Drupal's priority). 115 entries whose only in-week activity is the 2026-10-11 audit's own records are out of scope.

Coverage. Four re-sweeps (G1 to G3b) listed every in-week item; each carries a covered entry or a borderline-drop line in a week's run record, except Netcraft's calendar-invite phishing post of 2026-10-16, recovered as entries/2026-10-19/ics-calendar-invite-phishing-auto-added-outlook-gmail.md with tool:eviltokens registered and two product records for its affected products. All nine KEV additions of the week are covered.

Calibration. high passed 8 of 21 new entries (38%). Drupal SA-CORE-2026-014 fails the high bar and moves to notable; the rest hold, GitLab CVE-2026-97229 as a borderline. The monthly calibration section is in the 2026-10-11 report.

Warnings. One acknowledgment added: the 2026-10-11 audit's 198.2 h duration spans its eight-day pause on an API session limit. This record's own duration_seconds spans this fire's pause on the rate limit (2026-10-18T14:12Z to 2026-10-19T16:15Z) and is left visible for the next audit.

Budget (v4.21). 22 spawns before v4.21 landed (19 first spawns and three continuations after the rate limit, about 11.5 M sub-agent tokens; work/2026-10-18T1307Z-audit/budget.tsv), two above the new bound. The closing loop therefore ran the hard-invariant minimum, one verifier pass (the 23rd spawn, about 0.5 M tokens), recorded in verification.budget_cut. Seven of the 22 (D1 to D3, L and its continuation, T4, T5) were secondary work v4.21 reserves for operator-directed partial audits; their 188 out-of-week verdicts (77 factual errors) are carried forward unapplied.

Model baseline (Sonnet 5 → 5.5): verifier iterations 7.3 → 5.2, confirmed CLEAN 3/9 → 6/18, iteration-1 truth findings per entry 0.77 → 1.53, research median 9 → 22 min with 2.4 → 6.1 items. Recommendation: keep xhigh on research and verifier, try high on the main agent.

Verification: one cold pass of cti-verification walked all 89 claims of its scope (the new entry whole, this fire's changed claims on the 15 updated entries, the run record and the report) and returned NEEDS_FIXES with four truth findings: an unsupported "does not run periodically" in the Citrix correction, an undercounted registry change (three records, not one), a Copeland clause cited to CISA that only Claroty states, and a Bricksforge citation date. All four and seven of the eight advisory findings were fixed after the pass; two pre-existing advisories (Exchange's 2026-10-16 citation, Ivanti's contradiction wording) are carried forward. The spent budget ended the loop there (verification.budget_cut), so the fixes are not re-verified and the residual is 4.

2026-10-18T0256Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 2 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

Window: gap 24.0 h from 2026-10-17T0256Z-intel, window 26 h, developing-story window 72 h; the container clock agreed with the network date (skew 0 s) and the first fetch of origin/main was current. The window is a Saturday into Sunday and thin. Two new entries and three changelog records. New: ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick), high, a vendor-held Microsoft 365 application credential used against 162 or more customer tenants with directory-role self-assignments in about 50 tenants and added credentials in one (S3 and S4 surfaced it independently, merged on one incident key; Admiralty A1); Rank Math SEO PRO 3.0.123, notable, a vendor-confirmed backdoor in packages served for about eleven hours, kept short on precedent (the store carries the ShapedPlugin and Awesome Motive WordPress supply-chain entries) and single-source-victim because Wordfence only relays the vendor. Records: Danfoss and refrigeration controllers (update: CERT-FR's third version of 2026-10-16 changes the compromised-unit sequence to restart first and adds the whole-configuration check, and the Dixell France operator guide gives the XWEB PRO firmware boundary and the factory Admin account; the Detection line, summary and actions were rewritten where they stood), AhsayCBS (improvement: Horizon3's root cause and server-side hunt artifacts, first covered through the horizon3-ai lookback), Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88771 (improvement: Zscaler's first-party telemetry adds a Perl CGI handler and a FreeBSD binary delivery; the Magento infrastructure overlap is Zscaler's own lead, not attribution).

KEV sweep (work/2026-10-18T0256Z-intel/kev-window.txt): no CISA KEV addition inside the window (catalogue 2026.10.16 of 2026-10-16 is the newest S1 read), so no NOT COVERED, MENTION-ONLY, COVERED-STALE or RANSOMWARE row. S1 confirmed that no covered CVE moved from not-exploited to exploited and that the ENISA exploited list is fully covered.

Backlog (state/coverage_backlog.md): the one open row, Beyond Gravity, was re-gated on today's facts by S2: nothing newer than the SRF report of 2026-10-15, the vector, behaviour and data class are still not public, so an incident entry would carry no evidence-bound technique. Held unchanged on its named condition (BACS, the company or reporting names a vector, an actor or the data affected), expiry 2026-10-20; nothing changed state, so no note was appended.

borderline-drop lines:

  • borderline-drop: Keycloak 26.8.1 (S1; 19 CVEs) - advisories read are Low or Moderate, EPSS 0.0044 or below, no exploitation or KEV listing, so the regular patch cycle covers it; the SAML HTTP-Redirect signature parser differential has no CVE and rests on an issue title.
  • borderline-drop: Zimbra 10.1.21 advisory table (S1) - the vendor table and heise are 2026-10-01 and 2026-09-29, outside the window, with no exploitation; the password-recovery, WebDAV and OnlyOffice rows carry no CVE or severity, and the covered Zimbra entry already directs readers to 10.1.21. Reopen on Rapid7's next part or a CVE with severity.
  • borderline-drop: October Windows updates default the NTLMv1-derived single sign-on block to Enforce (S3; Microsoft KB5066470) - a vendor hardening default with an outage consequence, no attacker behaviour to map, outside the window; an operations notice, not a hunt, patch or block decision.
  • borderline-drop: IDC Frontier sixth report of 2026-10-18 (S4) - service-status change only on a routine, out-of-region entry; no new cause, route or actor.
  • borderline-drop: FBI PSA I-101326-PSA on North Korean IT-worker facilitators (S2) - US-written, no Swiss nexus, adds little to the three covered DPRK IT-worker entries.
  • borderline-drop: FBI and CISA PSA on election and campaign officials, heise's CDU Heilbronn mailbox hijack, Europol's digital-forensics report, Truesec commentary, Arkadia RAIDEN (S2, S3) - US-midterm or German party focus, no vector or actor, or commentary without telemetry; incident floor.
  • borderline-drop: German universities (Halle-Wittenberg, HU Berlin, LMU), the ChimeraZ burst of French forum claims, the Atexo/Docaposte supplier breach, Eurofiber France, Inter-Etab, ABC Bank, Eichstätt, Brenner Base Tunnel (Everest claim), the French hacktivist DDoS wave, ETS California, Cyber Daily exclusives, BAE Systems (S4) - claims without victim statements (PD-6), no vector or actor (incident floor), or out of nexus.
  • borderline-drop: Elastic Apex Accelerator, Group-IB KGB RAT, Report URI skimmer write-ups, Noma SneakPeek, Any.Run lure statistics, Unit 42's monthly ranking, Volexity part 3, the MALFEX npm package, iVerify recap, The Register on building automation, CSA Lab notes (S3) - no constituency nexus, no new behaviour, or vendor statistics.
  • borderline-drop: Fortinet FG-IR-26-176 to -185, the October Microsoft, Adobe and Palo Alto remainders, Juniper JSA112186, Chrome 155, phpMyFAQ 4.1.9, HPE ClearPass, Splunk SVD-2026-1006 (S1) - none exploited and none KEV-listed; unchanged calls on the facts earlier fires used. Splunk says its advisories publish 2026-10-21, so splunk-advisories should be rotated into S1 on 2026-10-21 or 2026-10-22.

Single-source and carve-outs: Rank Math is single-source-victim (the vendor discloses its own distribution incident and Wordfence relays it; Admiralty A2); the Horizon3 and Zscaler additions are first-party analyses of their own reverse engineering and telemetry and carry no verification change on their entries. Reduced-confidence inclusions: none. Identifier omission: Wordfence's page lists CVE-2026-111862 for the Rank Math incident, but the NVD API returned no record and the CVE Services API a 404 on 2026-10-18T03:27Z, so no cves[] record was written for it.

Contradictions: Huntress's count of 162 confirmed tenants (as of 2026-10-16 19:00 UTC) is the number cited; The Hacker News reports 173 for Huntress and the entry does not repeat it. Todyl's post is dated 2026-10-15 on its page yet references ConnectWise's advisory of 2026-10-16, so it was updated after first publication; the entry cites the page date and says Huntress and Todyl run living posts.

Source-recipe notes (for the next audit): ConnectWise's Trust Center page and Wordfence's blog were read through the metered reader (extract fell to jina); S2 spent about five reader fallbacks, four of them on guessed feed paths, which the source records now describe. The Dixell France guide is undated; the 2026-10-13 date given is the file's last modification on the vendor's server (HEAD request), disclosed in the Danfoss entry's sourcing note.

Coverage gaps: prodaft (no dated listing on any transport), apa-ots (no listing or feed route), hpe-networking-psirt (single advisory readable, no listing), hu-berlin.de notice (Anubis challenge, read only as quoted by borncity).

Essential-coverage: all 21 essential records were attempted and returned content; ncsc-ch-security-hub was an edit scan with no post edited since 2026-10-16T06:56Z.

Excluded as recent attempts: 90 standard or candidate records were held out of the rotation slices because the previous two fires attempted them (belt and braces over the rotation cursor); S4's slice took the twelve oldest-cursor breach and ransomware sources regardless, because that pool is small and entirely attempted by the previous two fires.

Self-identification: main agent Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) from the harness-injected model line; all four research sub-agents reported Sonnet 5.5 from their own prompt line.

Verification: four iterations. Iteration 1 (NEEDS_FIXES, 8 truth and 6 editorial findings, 17 with the advisories) and iteration 2 (NEEDS_FIXES, 5 truth) were fixed in place; iterations 3 and 4 are two consecutive CLEAN verdicts from independent cold passes, the second a full-ledger confirmation (141 of 141 claims). After iteration 4 the main agent applied three trivial wording fixes from its advisories (dropped 'paid' from the Rank Math summary, 'the malicious host Rank Math names', a missing verb in the Danfoss update section), none changing a sourced claim, and declined the other five advisories with the reasons recorded on the iteration. The Trust Center page for ConnectWise returned 403 to every live transport in the later passes, so those claims were checked against the body the gate saved at 2026-10-18T03:36Z.

Source health: tools/source_health.py probed 249 records, 247 relevant, one stale (threatpost, a demoted record) and one unreadable; the one UNSOLVED row, znuny-advisories (a candidate that has never been fetched), is a host outage: the site answers HTTP 503 to WebFetch and resets the connection from the container, so the recipe is unchanged and a note says to re-probe next fire.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-10-17
item.description: • GTIG: AOMEI update files were altered for minutes at a time to push a backdoor; Switzerland among victim countries. Google's GTIG and ManageEngine's METAL report that a cluster tracked as UNC7017 altered two configuration files on AOMEI's update servers for five to ten minutes at a time between April and July 2026, so any Backupper or AnyViewer client that polled during a window downloaded and ran the CROSSROAD downloader, which installed the SHINYROAD backdoor beside a signed Radmin binary. No software flaw is involved, GTIG names Switzerland among 11 victim countries, and the vendor's server-side repair does not clean a host that already ran the downloader, so installations need an endpoint hunt covering April to July 2026. →

AOMEI Backupper and AnyViewer update files tampered with for five to ten minutes at a time between April and July 2026 to push the CROSSROAD downloader and the SHINYROAD backdoor, with Switzerland among 11 countries GTIG names

GTIG and Mandiant report that a cluster they track as UNC7017 repeatedly altered two configuration files on AOMEI Technology's update servers between April and July 2026, each time for five to ten minutes before restoring the genuine content; GTIG confirmed three windows and says more probably went unseen (GTIG, 2026-10-16). ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab (METAL) writes "There was no CVE, no memory corruption, and no unpatched component." (METAL, 2026-10-16).

The client polls down_html.ini (update archive address and MD5 checksum) and Notifycfg.ini (what to display and run); during a window the actor pointed the first at an attacker-controlled ZIP with a matching checksum and padded the second with more than 35,000 lines of dummy sections, so the client started the unpacked downloader from its html directory, and GTIG describes the same flow for AnyViewer (GTIG, 2026-10-16). METAL's EDR recorded the chain on Backupper 8.3.0 (METAL, 2026-10-16).

The downloader, CROSSROAD, stops in some branches when the host geolocates to China (GTIG, 2026-10-16) and, METAL adds, when specific endpoint security agents are present (METAL, 2026-10-16). It registers a scheduled task that runs a signed Radmin binary every three hours; that binary loads an attacker-built DLL by search-order hijacking, which registers an in-process COM server running the SHINYROAD backdoor as encrypted PocketPy bytecode (GTIG, 2026-10-16). On some hosts GTIG later saw the Adaptix C2 agent, disguised as Nitro PDF tooling and started by hidden PowerShell through a second scheduled task (GTIG, 2026-10-16). The 20 July window also pointed a popup at a remote WebDAV path through an invisible window, which can leak the user's NetNTLMv2 response (GTIG, 2026-10-16).

GTIG's telemetry shows affected IT-services, telecommunications and higher-education organizations in 11 countries including Switzerland and calls the targeting opportunistic; AOMEI told Mandiant on 2026-07-29 that it had taken corrective action (GTIG, 2026-10-16). AOMEI's Backupper release notes through 8.5.0 list no change to update verification as of 2026-10-17 (AOMEI Technology, 2026-10-09).

Exposure
Windows hosts running AOMEI Backupper or AnyViewer that polled for updates during an unseen window between April and July 2026; server-side repair does not clean a host that already ran the downloader (GTIG, 2026-10-16).
Detection
In process telemetry, an executable written into the Tmphtml or html folders and started by the notification process, and a signed Radmin binary loading an unexpected DLL (GTIG, 2026-10-16); METAL adds dllhost.exe hosting a COM component registered from a non-standard path (METAL, 2026-10-16). Also scheduled tasks named RadminComponentRuntime or NitroRuntime, and outbound SMB (TCP 445) and WebDAV to external addresses; hunt the whole April to July span and preserve the cached update files in the Tmphtml folder (GTIG, 2026-10-16).

Triage: do not validate an alert by fetching AOMEI's update address now: the files revert within minutes and the genuine content served then has led analysts to dismiss real detections; the Nitro PDF camouflage can make alerts read as isolated user downloads, so trace each one's parent process back to the updater (GTIG, 2026-10-16). Radmin is legitimate software, so provenance discriminates: METAL's EDR recorded the updater's unsigned child process installing it (METAL, 2026-10-16).

Defender takeaway
Hunt every Windows host that runs AOMEI Backupper or AnyViewer for these artifacts even though AOMEI says its servers are repaired, treat a match as a compromised host, and block outbound SMB and WebDAV to external addresses, which GTIG advises against NTLM credential coercion (GTIG, 2026-10-16).

CVE-2026-82078 / CVE-2026-81578, PaperCut NG/MF: an Apache Tapestry request-routing confusion chains an unauthenticated config rewrite to arbitrary code execution, exploited before a patch existed

First published 2026-08-29 · open finding →

Update17 Oct 2026 03:38 UTCrun 2026-10-17T0256Z-inteltitlesummaryregionstechniquescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Hunt.io recovered the attacker's open directories (2026-10-15) and reports a second route to code execution through PaperCut's XML-RPC API that does not use the Tapestry bypass and works when the API allowlist is too permissive or no explicit token is set, a cron-kept reverse SOCKS tunnel, an offline LSA-secret playbook and 45 victims with live internal pivots, Switzerland among the countries listed. Hunt.io does not report the XML-RPC route used against a victim; PaperCut's documentation names the token and allowlist settings that close it. PaperCut's September bulletin, revised 2026-10-13, now lists CVE-2026-82077 as fixed in 24.1.10 and names 24.1.11 as the v24 build.

Hunt.io found three open directories on one attacker host and reconstructs the operator's toolkit from the files in them; it says the recovered material aligns with GreyNoise's published account of the AI-driven campaign (Hunt.io, 2026-10-15). The operator's notes record a second route to code execution that does not use the Tapestry bypass: PaperCut's XML-RPC API at /rpc/api/xmlrpc accepts api.setConfigValue when its network allowlist is too permissive or no explicit API token is configured, because the handler then falls back to the built-in admin password as the token, and the same user-lookup settings are then rewritten (Hunt.io, 2026-10-15). Hunt.io says an instance already hardened against the Tapestry bypass is not necessarily protected against this one if its XML-RPC API is exposed with weak access controls (Hunt.io, 2026-10-15); it does not report the route used against a victim. PaperCut's documentation says the API's authentication token should be defined in the advanced config key auth.webservices.auth-token and that the address allowlist can be set in the admin interface or through auth.webservices.allowed-addresses (PaperCut Software, 2026-01-30).

The files also show what follows a compromise. A Linux kit keeps a chisel reverse SOCKS5 client alive through cron entries (periodic and at reboot) and a watchdog script that checks the process (Hunt.io, 2026-10-15). The Windows playbook exports the SECURITY and SYSTEM registry hives from a compromised host to recover LSA secrets, the domain machine account's password among them, offline (Hunt.io, 2026-10-15). The scale comes from the actor's own files: a reconnaissance pool of 1,005 hosts in at least 45 countries (800 confirmed vulnerable and 205 flagged from version fingerprinting), 2,165 logged attempts, 46 Active Directory domains packaged as victim data and 45 targets with a live reverse SOCKS5 pivot at the time of capture (Hunt.io, 2026-10-15). Switzerland is among the countries listed for those 45 targets, with no sector or organisation named, and Hunt.io says it shared its findings and the victim data with the national CERTs of the affected countries (Hunt.io, 2026-10-15).

PaperCut's September security bulletin, last updated 2026-10-13, now lists CVE-2026-82077 as fixed in 24.1.10 on the 24.x branch as well as in 26.0.5 and 25.0.13, and recommends 26.0.5, 25.0.13 or 24.1.11 or later (PaperCut Software, 2026-09-24).

Sources: PaperCut Software (vendor security bulletin) · Huntress · Rapid7 · CERT-FR (ANSSI) advisory CERTFR-2026-AVI-1095 · NCSC-NL advisory NCSC-2026-0334 · GreyNoise · CISA KEV · watchTowr Labs · PaperCut Software (September security bulletin) · Hunt.io · PaperCut Software (product documentation)
